text:
How to use the catalogue
Start with a format family, then choose a ruleset. Versions with different setup or victory rules have their own pages. Rules pages contain the actual format procedures; parent pages help you choose between them.
A boxed set is a personal play kit built around a particular ruleset. Its page names that ruleset and records the box's additions, replacements, and optional rules. Drafts show the decisions that still need to be made.
Normal Magic rules apply unless a format changes them. See Using the rules for shared conventions and the difference between a recorded rule and an open design question.
This is a fan-made catalogue. The boxed sets are personal play kits, not commercial products.

title: Archenemy Commander
text:
Archenemy Commander
Archenemy versions · Rules: Commander team game
Players and materials
Choose one archenemy and a hero team, normally three or more heroes. Every player uses a legal Commander deck: 100 cards including the commander or commanders, the applicable color identity, and singleton construction except basic lands and explicit card exceptions.
The archenemy needs a scheme deck of at least ten cards with different English names. Prepare the tokens, counters, and commander-damage records required by the decks.
Setup
Choose the archenemy and hero team.
Put each player's commander or commanders in their command zone. Shuffle ordinary libraries.
Shuffle the archenemy's scheme deck and keep it face down in the command zone.
The archenemy starts at 60 life. The hero team starts with one shared total of 60 life, regardless of the number of heroes.
Each player draws seven and takes normal multiplayer mulligans.
The archenemy takes the first turn.
Commander tax, commander-zone movement, and commander damage remain in effect.
Turns and combat
The archenemy takes the first turn and draws during their first draw step. Then the hero team takes a shared turn. Alternate archenemy turns and team turns.
During a team turn, heroes move through the phases and steps together. Each untaps their own permanents, takes their own draw, and may use their own land play. They make their own decisions, pay their own costs, and keep their own hands, libraries, mana, and permanents. Being teammates does not let them spend one another's mana or cards.
The heroes declare their attacks together against the archenemy or legal objects that can be attacked. When the archenemy attacks, declare which hero or attackable object each creature attacks. Heroes declare blockers together and can use their creatures to defend a teammate or that teammate's planeswalker. They cannot attack one another.
Use the shared-team-turn rules for priority, simultaneous decisions, and combat. Individual card restrictions still apply; being on a team does not allow an otherwise illegal target or block.
Shared hero life and individual resources
Damage, life gain, and life loss affect the relevant player, then change the shared hero life total. A spell affecting each player or each opponent affects each hero separately; do not count the entire hero team as one target.
For example, if each of three heroes loses 2 life, their shared total falls by 6.
A cost or effect asking for a hero's life total uses the shared total. Paying life spends that shared resource; simultaneous life payments cannot exceed it. Setting one hero's life total adjusts the shared total accordingly. When an effect would set every hero's life, the team chooses one member to be affected. Teammates cannot exchange life totals with one another; redistribution can affect at most one member per team.
An effect preventing a hero from gaining life prevents the team's members from gaining life. An effect preventing a hero from losing life prevents team life loss and nonzero life payments. Apply the detailed shared-life rules in CR 810.9 for these interactions.
Poison counters are individual, with a threshold of ten, rather than the shared fifteen-poison rule from Two-Headed Giant. Record commander damage separately for each commander and each damaged player; do not pool damage from different commanders or different heroes.
Setting schemes in motion
Keep the scheme deck shuffled, face down in the command zone, separate from the ordinary library. Its owner cannot inspect or rearrange it without an effect allowing that.
As the archenemy's precombat main phase begins on each of their turns, turn the top scheme face up in the command zone. This mandatory turn-based action sets the scheme in motion and does not use the stack. Abilities that trigger from it do use the stack, so players can respond to those abilities.
Choose targets when putting a triggered ability on the stack. Make choices or payments that the effect asks for during resolution at that time, rather than while revealing the scheme.
Schemes stay in the command zone. They are not battlefield permanents, cannot be cast, and cannot be destroyed with an effect that destroys a permanent. A face-up scheme's abilities function from the command zone.
Non-ongoing schemes
A face-up, non-ongoing scheme goes face down on the bottom of its owner's scheme deck as a state-based action once no scheme triggered abilities are on the stack or waiting to be put there. Countering its ability does not leave the scheme permanently face up.
Ongoing schemes
An ongoing scheme stays face up until an ability tells its controller to abandon it. Abandoning it turns it face down and puts it on the bottom of its owner's scheme deck. Its printed condition determines when that happens; revealing another scheme does not automatically abandon it.
Follow individual scheme instructions for additional schemes, costs, choices, and exceptions. A scheme asking an opponent to choose “self” or “others” still permits “others” when that opponent has no teammates, even if that option affects nobody.
Winning and losing
Defeat the opposing side. This version uses the shared-life team win/loss rules referenced by CR 904.13b and 810.8: a team wins or loses together, including when one of its members wins or loses through an effect or another ordinary loss condition. A shared life total of zero or less causes the hero team to lose unless an applicable effect prevents it.
CR 904.13c specifically replaces shared poison with individual counters and the ten-counter threshold. Ordinary Commander damage remains a loss condition. Effects preventing a team member from winning or losing affect that team's result under the team rules. Conceding follows those team rules as well.
If both sides lose simultaneously, the game is a draw.
Other versions and references
Standard Archenemy uses separate hero life totals and a larger scheme deck. Commander Supervillain Rumble gives every player schemes in a free-for-all.
Sources: Wizards' Archenemy Commander rules and Comprehensive Rules 903, 904.13, 810.8, and 810.9.

title: Commander Supervillain Rumble
text:
Commander Supervillain Rumble
Archenemy versions · Rules: Commander free-for-all
Players and materials
Play a free-for-all Commander game, normally with three or more players. Everyone has their own scheme deck.
Each player supplies a legal 100-card Commander deck, including its commander or commanders, with normal singleton and color-identity requirements. Each scheme deck contains at least ten cards, all with different English names.
Setup
Put commanders in the command zone and shuffle ordinary libraries.
Shuffle scheme decks separately and keep them face down in their owners' command zones.
Set every player's individual life total to 40.
Randomly choose the starting player.
Draw seven cards each and take normal multiplayer mulligans.
The 60-life team setup from Archenemy Commander does not apply to this free-for-all version.
Turns, combat, and Commander rules
Take individual turns in normal turn order. Everyone is an opponent; nobody shares turns, life, or resources. The starting player draws on their first turn.
At the beginning of each player's precombat main phase, that player sets a scheme in motion. In the procedure below, “the archenemy” means that active player.
Attack any legal opponent or attackable object, assigning each attacker separately. Players may attack several opponents in one combat, but cannot block for another opponent. Commander tax, command-zone movement, and the 21-combat-damage loss condition from a single commander apply normally.
Setting schemes in motion
Keep the scheme deck shuffled, face down in the command zone, separate from the ordinary library. Its owner cannot inspect or rearrange it without an effect allowing that.
As the archenemy's precombat main phase begins on each of their turns, turn the top scheme face up in the command zone. This mandatory turn-based action sets the scheme in motion and does not use the stack. Abilities that trigger from it do use the stack, so players can respond to those abilities.
Choose targets when putting a triggered ability on the stack. Make choices or payments that the effect asks for during resolution at that time, rather than while revealing the scheme.
Schemes stay in the command zone. They are not battlefield permanents, cannot be cast, and cannot be destroyed with an effect that destroys a permanent. A face-up scheme's abilities function from the command zone.
Non-ongoing schemes
A face-up, non-ongoing scheme goes face down on the bottom of its owner's scheme deck as a state-based action once no scheme triggered abilities are on the stack or waiting to be put there. Countering its ability does not leave the scheme permanently face up.
Ongoing schemes
An ongoing scheme stays face up until an ability tells its controller to abandon it. Abandoning it turns it face down and puts it on the bottom of its owner's scheme deck. Its printed condition determines when that happens; revealing another scheme does not automatically abandon it.
Follow individual scheme instructions for additional schemes, costs, choices, and exceptions. A scheme asking an opponent to choose “self” or “others” still permits “others” when that opponent has no teammates, even if that option affects nobody.
Winning, losing, and leaving
Win by being the last remaining player or through a normal winning effect. Individual loss conditions include zero life, ten poison counters, drawing from an empty library, and 21 combat damage from a single commander.
When a player leaves, their owned objects, including schemes, leave under the ordinary multiplayer rules. Remaining players continue; if all remaining players lose together, the game is a draw.
References
Wizards' Archenemy Commander page, Supervillain Rumble section and Comprehensive Rules 903 and 904.

title: Supervillain Rumble
text:
Supervillain Rumble
Archenemy versions · Rules: constructed free-for-all
Players and materials
This is the free-for-all version of Archenemy, normally for three or more players. Every player is an archenemy and supplies:
An ordinary constructed deck of at least 60 cards, following the agreed card pool and normal copy limits.
A separate scheme deck of at least 20 cards, with no more than two cards of any one English name.
Required tokens, counters, and life-tracking aids.

Keep each scheme deck face down in its owner's command zone.
Every player starts at 40 life.
Randomly determine the starting player.
Draw seven cards each and take normal multiplayer mulligans.

Each player sets a scheme in motion at the beginning of their own precombat main phase. In the procedure below, “the archenemy” means the player whose turn it is.
Players may attack multiple opponents in the same combat, choosing the defending player or other legal attack destination for each creature. You cannot block for another opponent. Apply ordinary free-for-all rules.

Keep the scheme deck shuffled, face down in the command zone, separate from the ordinary library. Its owner cannot inspect or rearrange it without an effect allowing that.

Follow individual scheme instructions for additional schemes, costs, choices, and exceptions. A scheme asking an opponent to choose “self” or “others” still permits “others” when that opponent has no teammates, even if that option affects nobody.

Win by being the last remaining player or through a normal winning effect. Ordinary Magic loss conditions apply, including zero life, ten poison counters, and drawing from an empty library.
When a player leaves, their owned cards, including their schemes, leave the game; apply the rest of the multiplayer leaving rules. The surviving players continue. Simultaneous loss of all remaining players results in a draw.
References
Wizards' Supervillain Rumble rules and Comprehensive Rules 904.12.
For Commander decks and singleton scheme decks, use Commander Supervillain Rumble.

title: Standard Archenemy
text:
Standard Archenemy
Archenemy versions · Rules: traditional team game
Players and materials
Use one archenemy and a team of heroes. The published format recommends three or more heroes; the comprehensive rules allow a team of any size.
Each player supplies an ordinary constructed deck of at least 60 cards, using the group's agreed card pool and the normal four-copy limit except basic lands and card-specific exceptions. The archenemy also needs at least 20 scheme cards, with at most two cards of any one English name. Supply tokens and counters required by the cards.
Setup
Choose the archenemy and the hero team.
Shuffle every ordinary deck and the scheme deck separately.
Set the archenemy to 40 life and each hero to 20 life. Hero life totals are separate.
Draw seven cards each and take normal multiplayer mulligans.
Put the face-down scheme deck in the command zone. No scheme starts in motion unless another effect says so.
The archenemy takes the first turn.

Follow individual scheme instructions for additional schemes, costs, choices, and exceptions. A scheme asking an opponent to choose “self” or “others” still permits “others” when that opponent has no teammates, even if that option affects nobody.
Winning, losing, and leaving
The archenemy wins when every hero has lost. The hero team wins when the archenemy loses, including heroes who were eliminated earlier. If the archenemy and the last hero lose simultaneously, the game is a draw.
Each player's ordinary loss conditions still apply: zero or less life, drawing from an empty library, ten poison counters, or a relevant card effect. A hero losing does not eliminate the other heroes.
When a player leaves, remove their owned objects, end effects that gave them control of other players' objects, and apply the remaining multiplayer leaving-the-game rules. Do not simply leave an eliminated hero's creatures under the team's control.
Other versions and references
For Commander decks with shared hero life, use Archenemy Commander. For everyone having schemes, use Supervillain Rumble.
Sources: Wizards' format rules, original rules explanation, and Comprehensive Rules 314, 805, 808, and 904. The current mulligan procedure comes from normal Magic rules rather than the older article's historical wording.

title: Assassin
text:
Assassin
All formats
Assassin formats assign each player a secret target, mark, or quarry. This is different from BANG-like formats, which assign team or solo victory roles.
Rulesets
Ruleset
Contents
Hitmen
The local Pegasus Loft rules for Mark Cards, Spheres, attacking, targeting expansion, defensive responses, passing Marks, and Free Agents.
There is no single general Assassin ruleset recorded here. The Hitmen page preserves the actual local procedures and identifies unresolved interactions.
Other versions
Additional Assassin versions should receive their own rules pages and original source links. Their targeting or reward rules should not be folded into Hitmen without a deliberate house-rule change.

title: Hitmen
text:
Hitmen
Assassin parent page · Local rules: Pegasus Loft
Hitmen is a local variant of the broader Assassin format. Each player receives a secret Mark. Instead of a normal free-for-all, players can only attack or target their current Mark unless the rules below expand their legal targets.
Terminology
A Mark Card is the numbered card dealt to a player to indicate their assigned target.
A player's Mark is the player indicated by their current Mark Card.
A player's Sphere consists of that player and anything targetable that player controls. This includes permanents, tokens, spells and abilities on the stack, and any other targetable game object a card or rule may care about.
Setup
Mark Cards are numbered 1 through X, where X is the number of players.
Each player receives one Mark Card.
Each number corresponds to another player.
Targeting Rules
You may only attack your Mark.
Your spells and abilities may only target your Mark's Sphere.
If you do not have enough valid targets, you may also target the Spheres of players next to your Mark.
If you still do not have enough valid targets, continue expanding outward from the previous set of players until the effect can be completed or all players are included.
When an effect on the stack affects you or anything you control, even if it does not target, you may target that effect or its controller's Sphere until the stack resolves.
Changing Marks
When your Mark dies, take their Mark Card. That card indicates your new Mark.
If a player ever has their own number as a Mark Card, including during setup, they become a Free Agent and may attack or target anyone.
Win Condition
Be the last player standing.
As a shorter game option, the table may set a required number of kills instead.
Underlying game
Use the decks, starting life, opening hands, and normal turn structure of the base Magic format agreed by the group. Hitmen changes attacking, targeting, and assigned objectives; it does not supply a separate deck-construction format. For Commander games, ordinary commander rules still apply.
Decisions not yet recorded
The original local rules above are preserved. Before formalizing a boxed set, decide:
Whether self-targeting or targeting your own permanents should be an explicit exception to the Mark-only restriction. As written, the restriction and its expansion procedure apply to those targets too.
Whether attacking a Mark's planeswalker or a battle they protect is allowed; the current attack rule names only the Mark.
Whether the defensive-response permission lasts until the relevant object resolves or the entire stack empties. The original wording says “until the stack resolves.”
How to pass Mark Cards when multiple players die simultaneously or a Free Agent leaves.
For the optional shorter game, the exact kill count, how kill credit is assigned, and how ties are resolved.
These are questions for the local format, not extra restrictions or permissions silently added by this page.

title: BANG! Magic — Source Notes
text:
BANG! Magic — Source Notes
For the play procedure, open the dedicated rules page. These notes preserve source context and historical discussion.
Source: https://www.reddit.com/r/magicTCG/comments/1w81fm/bang_magic/
Original poster: Saporling Context: Reddit /r/magicTCG post, archived, roughly 2013.
This post describes a Commander/EDH multiplayer variant based on the hidden-role structure of the board game BANG!. The format adds secret objectives and table politics to a 5-7+ player game.
Setup
Before the game, write the roles on individual cards or tokens. Deal one role card to each player.
All roles are secret except the Sheriff. A player's role should normally be revealed only when that player dies.
Roles
Role
Count
Visibility
Objective
Sheriff
1
Public
Eliminate the Outlaws and the Renegade.
Deputy
1+
Secret
Help the Sheriff eliminate the Outlaws and the Renegade.
Outlaw
2+
Secret
Kill the Sheriff. If the Sheriff dies, the Outlaws win.
Renegade
1
Secret
Be the last player alive.
Sheriff Rules
The Sheriff starts with their role card revealed and takes the first turn.
The source notes that the Sheriff usually receives a buff as a house rule, often +20 starting life.
Renegade Notes
The Renegade is a solo role. The Renegade wants the game to reach a final showdown with the Sheriff, then win as the last player alive.
The source frames the Renegade as the role most dependent on politics: the Renegade must look useful to other factions, manipulate suspicion, and avoid letting the Outlaws win too early.
Discussion Notes
The comments are useful mostly for table-balance concerns:
Several commenters point out that the role structure comes from the board game BANG!
A correction clarifies that the Renegade does not win merely because the Sheriff dies; only the Outlaws win that way.
Commenters compare this format to Kingdoms, another EDH hidden-role variant.
The Renegade is discussed as a difficult but interesting role because they must weaken both sides without letting either side win too early.
Takeaways For Game-Night Boxes
This version is simple and easy to teach. It does not require custom cards beyond role indicators.
For a boxed set, the important pieces are:
Role cards.
A player-count chart.
A clear Sheriff bonus.
A reminder that the Renegade wins only by being the last player alive.
A table-talk policy that prevents players from proving their roles through out-of-game promises.

title: Kingdom / BANG EDH — Source Notes
text:
Kingdom / BANG EDH — Source Notes
For the play procedure, open the dedicated rules page. These notes preserve source context and historical discussion.
Source: https://www.mtgsalvation.com/forums/the-game/commander-edh/616543-kingdom-aka-bang-edh-a-variant-format
Original poster: kesofcom Context: MTGSalvation Commander/EDH forum thread, July 2015.
This source presents a 5-6 player Commander variant inspired by BANG! and Three Kingdoms-style hidden-role games.
Setup
This is a role-playing variant used with Commander decks. Each role has its own win condition, and some roles have additional rules.
Prepare a role-card set:
Role
Count
Emperor
1
Guard
1
Assassin
2
Rogue
1
For a 6-player game, add one additional Assassin.
Shuffle the role cards and deal one to each player. A player's role does not change during the game.
Role Visibility
The Emperor reveals their role.
All other roles stay secret and face down.
Roles are revealed only when a player dies or when the game ends.
Players cannot concede.
Table-Talk Rules
The source is explicit that players should not use out-of-game leverage to prove their roles.
Players may not make external promises such as "if I am lying, you can tear up my card."
Players also cannot talk about their role directly. They may discuss actions they have taken in the game, such as reminding another player that they destroyed a token army attacking them.
Role Table
Role
Win Condition
Bonus / Penalty
Emperor
The Emperor is alive, all Assassins are dead, and the Rogue is dead. The Guard's status does not affect the Emperor's win.
Starts first, +10 starting life, +1 starting hand size, +1 maximum hand size.
Guard
All Assassins are dead, the Rogue is dead, and the Emperor is not dead. The Guard can be dead and still win.
No listed bonus.
Assassin
The Emperor is dead, and the Rogue's win condition has not been fulfilled. Any or all Assassins can be dead and still win.
When an Assassin dies, the player who killed them may draw up to three cards.
Rogue
The Rogue is alive, all players except the Emperor and Rogue are alive, and the Rogue kills the Emperor.
Alternate condition: the Rogue may kill all other players at once if the Emperor is last or tied for last to die.
Emperor Penalty
If the Emperor kills the Guard, the Emperor exiles their nonland permanents, graveyard, and hand.
Rogue Redeal Rule
If a player was the Rogue in the previous game, they may request a redeal before the next game starts, until they are not the Rogue again.
Design Notes From The Thread
The discussion focuses heavily on making the Rogue playable and preventing role-proofing.
The poster notes:
A three-card reward for killing an Assassin is enough incentive without encouraging too much early killing.
The Emperor needs a meaningful penalty for killing the Guard, or the Emperor can stab blindly.
The Rogue is intentionally difficult but can be fun because it asks the player to manipulate the table.
Suggested Rogue strategies include:
Include a way to win in one strong turn, such as a large drain spell.
Increase spot removal and board wipes so the Rogue can help the Emperor and prolong the game.
Pretend to be the Guard, help kill the Assassins, then isolate the Emperor for the final duel.
Alternate Rogue Discussion
The thread discusses an alternate Rogue win condition where the Rogue wins by personally killing two players.
That creates rules complications if the Rogue's second kill is the Emperor, because the Assassin team might also be trying to win at that moment. The thread suggests avoiding simultaneous wins by ruling that:
The Rogue and Assassins cannot both win if the Rogue's second kill is the Emperor; or
The Rogue's second kill cannot be the Emperor.
Related Table Variants
Commenters mention simpler versions with roles such as:
King
Knight
Bandits
Assassin
The thread also mentions the format being known by names such as Empire and Usurper.
Takeaways For Game-Night Boxes
This version is more formal than the basic Reddit BANG! variant. It is useful if the box wants:
Clear anti-role-proofing rules.
A harsh Emperor penalty.
A reward for killing Assassins.
A Rogue role with explicit strategy and balance support.

title: Kingdoms: EDH Variant — Source Notes
text:
Kingdoms: EDH Variant — Source Notes
For the play procedure, open the dedicated rules page. These notes preserve source context and historical discussion.
Source: https://www.reddit.com/r/EDH/comments/1plyyj/kingdoms_edh_variant/
Original poster: TheChurchIsHere Context: Reddit /r/EDH post, roughly 2013.
Kingdoms is a hidden-role Commander variant for 5-6 players. It uses basic lands as role cards, which makes the format easy to assemble without printing custom components.
Components
In addition to each player's Commander deck, prepare these role cards:
Player Count
Role Cards
5
1 Plains, 1 Forest, 2 Mountains, 1 Swamp
6
1 Plains, 1 Forest, 2 Mountains, 1 Swamp, 1 Island
Shuffle the role cards and deal one face down to each player.
Role Table
Land
Role
Objective
Plains
King
Be the last player standing.
Forest
Knight
Protect the King. If the King and Knight are the last two players standing, both win.
Mountain
Bandit
Kill the King. If the King dies, the Bandits win, regardless of who remains.
Swamp
Assassin
Kill everyone.
Island
Usurper
Deal the killing blow to the King, become the new King, and continue from there.
Starting The Game
The King reveals themself, starts at 50 life, and goes first.
No other player may reveal their role card until the game is over, except when the Usurper kills the King. Players may claim to be a role, but they may not reveal the physical role card.
Usurper Rule
If the Usurper deals the killing blow to the King:
The Usurper becomes the new King.
The Usurper's life total becomes 50.
The former King remains in the game as the new Usurper at 1 life.
The Knight now protects the new King.
Political Shape
The post emphasizes that Kingdoms changes multiplayer politics. Previous grudges matter less because every player has a new secret incentive.
The Assassin role is difficult. Commenters describe the Assassin as wanting the game to go long, often pretending to be the Knight until the Bandits are contained and the King is vulnerable.
Discussion Notes
Useful comments from the thread include:
The format is repeatedly compared to BANG! in EDH form.
Several commenters discuss whether the Assassin is underpowered or simply demanding.
Some groups use alternate names such as King, Knight, Bandits, and Assassin.
Other groups add or replace roles, such as Traitor, Jester, or variants where the Usurper changes the throne.
Takeaways For Game-Night Boxes
Kingdoms is attractive because it needs almost no custom material. A boxed version could still improve the experience with:
Dedicated role cards.
A one-page role reminder.
A player-count setup chart.
A clearer Assassin strategy note.
Optional alternate-role modules for groups that dislike the default Assassin or Usurper balance.

title: MTG Treachery — Source Notes
text:
MTG Treachery — Source Notes
For the play procedure, open the dedicated rules page. These notes preserve source context and historical discussion.
Source: https://mtgtreachery.net/en/
MTG Treachery is a maintained fan-made multiplayer variant for Magic: The Gathering, optimized for Commander/EDH. It is in the same broad family as Kingdoms, Usurper, Throne Magic, Assassin, and BANG!-style variants.
The source site provides rules, printable Identity cards, a card oracle, web play tools, a Discord bot, and comprehensive rules.
Site Sections
Section
Purpose
How to Play
Introductory rules and role overview.
Game Materials
Printable Identity cards, tokens, and rule cards.
Banlist
Additional caution list beyond the base format's ban list.
Play by Web
Browser tools for playing without printed cards.
Play on Discord
Discord bot support.
Oracle
Searchable Identity card database.
Comprehensive Rules
Formal rules add-on for the Treachery variant.
Premise
Treachery adds a custom card type, Identity, to multiplayer Magic. Each player receives an Identity card that defines their role, allies, and win condition.
The format is built around table politics, bluffing, and secret information. Players can lie, hide their role, and choose when to reveal powerful one-shot abilities.
The source recommends Treachery for 5-7 players, though it supports 4 and 8+ players.
Roles
Role
Team / Objective
Leader
The Leader and Guardians win if they are the last players standing.
Guardian
Guardians help the Leader and win or lose with the Leader.
Assassin
Assassins win if the Leader is eliminated.
Traitor
The Traitor wins by being the last player standing.
The Traitor usually needs to remove the Assassins before eliminating the Leader, because if the Leader dies while an Assassin can claim victory, the Assassin team wins.
Identity Cards
Identity cards are custom nontraditional Magic cards. They remain in the command zone throughout the game.
An Identity's subtype defines the player's role. Except for the Leader, Identities are usually secret and face down.
Most non-Leader Identities have an Unveil ability. Unveiling turns the Identity face up and triggers a powerful ability, but it also reveals the player's role.
Players are considered opponents to each other while their Identity cards are face down.
Starting A Game
Prepare an Identity deck based on player count, shuffle it, and deal one Identity face down to each player. Each player secretly looks at their Identity. The Leader reveals themself and starts the game.

Banlist Notes
Treachery is meant to be played alongside another multiplayer format, usually Commander. It follows the banned/restricted list of the base format.
The source additionally suggests avoiding a few cards unless the table agrees ahead of time. The concern is that Treachery's political structure and universal starting-opponent status can make some cards especially disruptive.
Additional suggested avoids:

Digital Tools
The source mentions:
MTG Cloak as a newer web application for playing Treachery without printed cards.

A Treachery Discord bot with /help support.
Comprehensive Rules Summary
The comprehensive rules are presented as an add-on to the official Magic Comprehensive Rules. They are not intended to be read from beginning to end; they are a reference for specific rules questions.
Important concepts include:
Identity is a custom card type used only for Treachery.
Identity cards remain in the command zone.
Identity cards are not permanents and cannot be cast or included in a deck.
Identity subtypes are also called identity types or roles.
The identity types are Leader, Guardian, Assassin, and Traitor.
The Leader subtype includes a static ability that makes its controller the starting player.
Face-down Identity cards have no characteristics.
A player may look at their own face-down Identity, but not another player's face-down Identity unless an ability allows it.
Unveil
Unveil is the core reveal mechanic.
In practical terms:
Identity cards with Unveil can start face down in the command zone.
A player may unveil their face-down Identity when they have priority by paying its Unveil cost.
Unveiling is a special action and does not use the stack.
Many Identity cards trigger when unveiled.
When a player loses, their face-down Identity is revealed.
At the end of the game, all face-down Identities are revealed.
Undercover
Undercover is a special Unveil restriction, usually found on some Guardian Identities.
It generally means the Identity can be unveiled only if:
Another non-Leader Identity card has been revealed; or
A player other than you attacked a Leader player this game.
Treachery Rules Structure
The formal Treachery variant rules define:
A Treachery game as a multiplayer game with four or more players, best at five or six.
An Identity deck with exactly one Identity per player.
Exactly one Leader.
At least one Traitor.
Assassins equal to half the player count, rounded down.
Remaining slots filled by Guardians or Traitors.
The Identity distribution is known before the game begins.
Teams
Identity
Team
Leader
Leader team.
Guardian
Leader team.
Assassin
Assassin team.
Traitor
A solo team.
Face-down Identity
No teammates and considered opponents with other players until revealed.
Winning And Losing
The comprehensive rules specify:
A team loses if all players on that team have lost.
The Leader team loses if all Leaders have lost, even if Guardians remain.
The Assassin team wins if all Leaders have lost and at least one Assassin Identity remains in the game.
A Traitor wins if all of that Traitor's opponents have left the game, including other Traitors.
If any player on a team wins, their whole team wins.
Leaving The Game
When a player leaves the game:
Their face-down Identity must be revealed.
The game remembers their last known team.
Some Identity-related abilities or control-change effects may continue under the comprehensive rules.

title: BANG! Magic
text:
BANG! Magic
BANG-like versions · Rules: Saporling's Commander variant
Players and materials
This version is intended for five to seven or more players using Commander decks. Prepare one hidden role card per player. Tokens or slips of paper are sufficient.
Use exactly one Sheriff, exactly one Renegade, at least one Deputy, and at least two Outlaws. At five players this means 1 Sheriff, 1 Deputy, 2 Outlaws, and 1 Renegade. The source does not assign a fixed distribution for larger groups; agree how the extra Deputy/Outlaw slots are filled before dealing.
Setup
Choose Commander decks using ordinary Commander construction and legality.
Agree the role distribution and whether the Sheriff receives a house bonus.
Shuffle the role cards and deal one secretly to each player.
Each player looks only at their own role. The Sheriff turns their role face up; the other roles remain hidden.
Start at the usual Commander life total of 40, modified by the chosen Sheriff bonus.
Draw seven cards, take normal multiplayer mulligans, and start with the Sheriff's turn.
The original post describes +20 starting life as a usual house bonus, which gives the Sheriff 60 life. It is an optional choice, not a mandatory bonus specified for every game.
Turns and roles
Play normal individual Commander turns. Commander tax and commander damage still apply. Hidden allegiances do not by themselves give shared life totals, shared turns, or permission to block for another player.
Role
Objective
Sheriff
Survive while all Outlaws and the Renegade are eliminated.
Deputy
Help the Sheriff eliminate all Outlaws and the Renegade.
Outlaw
Eliminate the Sheriff.
Renegade
Be the only surviving player.
The Renegade must arrange a final confrontation with the Sheriff. Merely killing the Sheriff while other players remain does not give the Renegade a win.
Revealing roles
Keep your role card hidden until you die, except for the public Sheriff. Reveal it when eliminated. Politics and bluffing are part of play; knowing what someone claims does not change the role they actually received.
The source does not impose the separate table-talk restrictions from Kingdom / BANG EDH.
Ending the game
If the Sheriff survives and all Outlaws and the Renegade have been eliminated, the Sheriff and Deputies achieve their objective.
If the Sheriff dies before the Renegade can be the sole survivor, the game ends with an Outlaw win.
The Renegade wins only as the last living player. The source's corrected description specifically calls for a Sheriff-versus-Renegade finish.
Apply ordinary Magic loss conditions to determine who has been eliminated. The short source does not resolve simultaneous mass-elimination ties or every alternate-win-card interaction; agree those cases before using such cards rather than importing another hidden-role version's answer.
Optional rules and source boundaries
The Sheriff bonus is the original post's house-rule option. Comments discuss rewards for killing Outlaws and penalties for killing a Deputy, but those additions disagree across commenters and are not part of this posted ruleset. The separately documented Kingdom / BANG EDH version defines its own rewards and penalties.
Source: Saporling's BANG! Magic post and author-confirmed Renegade correction. Archived notes.

The source's Rogue condition says the other players are alive, while its strategy advice describes eliminating them and reaching a final duel. Both are recorded below. Choose an interpretation before play; this catalogue has not silently corrected the source into a new rule.

Setup
Prepare legal Commander decks and the listed role-card set.
Shuffle the roles and deal one to each player. Roles remain assigned for the entire game.
The Emperor reveals their card. Everyone else keeps theirs face down.
Each player starts at the normal Commander life total, except the Emperor receives +10 life, for 50.
The Emperor also receives +1 opening hand size and +1 maximum hand size, giving eight cards for each instead of seven.
Take normal multiplayer mulligans with those hand-size adjustments.
The Emperor takes the first turn.
Normal play and role visibility
Use ordinary individual Commander turns, combat, commander tax, and commander-damage rules. The roles create objectives rather than shared turns or shared resources.
Only the Emperor starts revealed. Reveal other roles when that player dies or the game ends. The source says players cannot concede; tables must decide before starting whether they intend to adopt that house restriction.
Table talk
Do not discuss your role directly. You may discuss your actions, such as pointing out that you removed creatures attacking the Emperor.
Do not make out-of-game promises or stakes to prove a role. For example, offering to let somebody damage a physical card if you are lying is outside the source's permitted table talk.
Role objectives
Emperor: remain alive while all Assassins and the Rogue are dead. The Guard may be alive or dead.
Guard: all Assassins and the Rogue must be dead, and the Emperor must remain alive. The Guard may die and still win.
Assassins: the Emperor must be dead and the Rogue's victory condition must not have been satisfied. Eliminated Assassins can still share the Assassin victory.
Rogue, literal posted condition: the Rogue is alive, every player other than the Emperor and Rogue is alive, and the Rogue kills the Emperor.
Rogue, posted alternate condition: the Rogue kills every other player at once, remains alive, and the Emperor is last or tied for last to die.
The literal Rogue wording conflicts with the same post's recommendation to remove the Assassins and reach a final duel. A table choosing “everyone else must be dead” is resolving that source ambiguity, not reading an unambiguous rule.
Elimination rewards and penalties
An Assassin dies
The player who killed that Assassin may draw up to three cards.
The Emperor kills the Guard
The Emperor exiles their nonland permanents, their graveyard, and their hand. This version says exile; do not replace it with another variant's sacrifice or discard penalty.
The source does not fully define kill credit for every simultaneous effect or concession. Agree how to handle such effects before relying on a reward or penalty.
Between games: Rogue redeal
A player who was the Rogue in the previous game may request that the next role deal be repeated until they are not the Rogue again. Resolve this before beginning the game.
Optional two-kill Rogue proposal
The discussion proposes a Rogue victory for personally killing two players. It also identifies a conflict if the second victim is the Emperor. A group adopting this proposal must choose its additional restriction: either the second victim cannot be the Emperor, or a specific priority rule must prevent a simultaneous Rogue/Assassin victory. This is an unfinished alternate proposal, not part of the default role objectives.
Source: kesofcom's Kingdom / BANG EDH thread. Archived notes.

Setup

Each player secretly looks at their card.
The King reveals their role and starts at 50 life. Everyone else starts at the normal Commander total of 40.
Prepare Commander libraries and command zones, draw seven cards, and take normal multiplayer mulligans.
The King takes the first turn.
Play normal individual Commander turns. Commander tax and the normal 21-combat-damage threshold remain in effect; the King does not receive an increased commander-damage threshold.
Roles and victory conditions
Role
Full objective
King
Be the last survivor, or finish as the last two players with the Knight.
Knight
Protect the current King. If the King and Knight are the last two players, both win.
Bandit
Eliminate the King. The Bandits win when the King dies, regardless of which Bandits remain. The Usurper's role exchange is the special exception below.
Assassin
Eliminate everyone else and be the last survivor.
Usurper
Personally deliver the killing blow to the King, take the throne, and continue pursuing the King's objective. Taking the throne does not itself end the game.
The King and Knight's allegiance does not create shared turns, shared life, or permission to block for one another. Ordinary free-for-all rules still govern the actual cards.
Role secrecy
Except for the King and a Usurper taking the throne, players may not reveal their role card until the game ends. They may claim a role, truthfully or falsely, but may not show the card as proof.
Unlike BANG! Magic, this source does not tell an eliminated player to reveal their card immediately.
Usurping the throne
If the Usurper delivers the killing blow to the King:
The Usurper reveals their role.
Exchange the King and Usurper roles.
The new King goes to 50 life.
The former King remains in the game as the new Usurper at 1 life.
The Knight's objective becomes protecting the new King.
Continue the game instead of awarding the Bandits a victory for that exchange.
This rule changes roles and life totals. It does not say to restart the game or exchange decks, hands, or permanents.
Commander-damage and poison option
In a later reply, the original poster says their group resets commander damage or poison when one of those conditions lets the Usurper defeat the King. They explicitly describe this as varying by table. Decide whether to use that reset before play; without a rule addressing the lethal counters or damage, changing a life total alone does not cure that loss condition.
Cases the source leaves open
The post does not fully define “killing blow” for simultaneous eliminations, concessions, shared effects, or non-damage loss conditions. It also does not establish a general priority rule for alternate-win cards. Record those choices before a game that can produce them.
The other roles suggested in the comments, such as the Fool, are separate house-rule proposals. They are not extra roles in the five- and six-player distributions above.

MTG Treachery
BANG-like versions · Rules: published Treachery rules, May 3, 2026
Treachery adds Identity cards to an underlying multiplayer format, usually Commander. This page records the setup, Identity rules, unveil procedure, team rules, and end-of-game exceptions. Individual Identity abilities still use their card text.
Players, decks, and materials
Play with at least four players. The introductory page recommends five to seven; the comprehensive rules describe five or six as ideal.
Choose the underlying format and decks before preparing the Identity deck. For Commander, use normal Commander decks, command zones, commander tax, and commander damage. Treachery uses free-for-all turns, allows attacks against multiple players, and uses neither limited range of influence nor the deploy-creatures option.
Prepare exactly one Identity card per player. Identity rarity indicates complexity rather than power: uncommon is recommended for first games, rare for advanced play, mythic for expert play, and purple/special for deliberately chaotic identities.
Preparing the Identity deck
The general construction rule calls for exactly one Leader, at least one Traitor, and Assassins equal to half the player count rounded down. Fill the remaining places with Guardians or Traitors.
The source also publishes this recommended table:

The published eight-player row uses three Assassins; the general half-rounded-down formula gives four. Both appear in the current source. Choose the recommended row or a formula-based distribution before preparing an eight-player game, and announce the distribution. Do not accidentally combine them.
The role distribution is public information before the game, except in the optional Backstab Rumble setup below.
Setup
Choose decks, the Identity selection, and the role distribution.
Shuffle the Identity deck and deal one Identity face down to each player.
Players privately inspect their own Identity.
Put each Identity in its owner's command zone. An Identity with unveil starts face down; an Identity without unveil starts face up.
Prepare the underlying game. Starting life is 20, or 40 for Commander, unless an Identity or the underlying format changes it. The normal opening hand is seven, subject to those same exceptions.
The player with the face-up Leader Identity takes the first turn. If effects designate several starting players, randomly choose among them.
Other roles remain secret while their Identities are face down. Do not reveal one just to prove a claim.
Identity cards and abilities
Identity is a nontraditional card type. An Identity:
Stays in the command zone for the entire game. If it would leave that zone, it remains there.
Is not a permanent, cannot be cast, and does not go into an ordinary deck.
Can be introduced from outside the game by an effect that specifically permits it.
Is initially owned by the player who started with it in their command zone, and controlled by that owner.
Can have multiple Identity subtypes: Leader, Guardian, Assassin, and Traitor.
Has no characteristics while face down.
Can be inspected by its controller at any time. Other players cannot inspect it without permission from an effect.
A face-up Identity's static, activated, and triggered abilities function from the command zone. An ability referring to “this identity” refers to its own source card there. A reference to a particular role's “player” means a player controlling a face-up Identity with that subtype. Some abilities modify the pregame procedure itself.
Unveil: complete procedure
An unveil ability makes the Identity start face down and makes it turn face up when its controller loses.
To unveil voluntarily:
Wait until you have priority.
Check any restriction on the Identity, including undercover.
Show what the Identity's unveil cost would be face up.
Choose any required value of X and pay that cost.
Turn the Identity face up. Its normal characteristics return.
Put any abilities triggered by this unveil onto the stack at the appropriate time.
Unveiling is a special action. It does not use the stack and cannot itself be responded to. The triggered abilities produced by it do use the stack and can be responded to.
An Identity without an unveil cost cannot be turned face up using this procedure. If another ability refers to X in the unveil cost, it uses the value chosen while unveiling.
An “as this Identity is unveiled” effect applies during the turn-face-up action. A “when unveiled” ability triggers only from turning it face up through the unveil special action; merely revealing it on elimination does not perform that action.
Undercover
An undercover restriction permits unveiling only after at least one of these has happened:
Another non-Leader Identity has been revealed.
A player other than you has attacked a Leader player this game.
For the second condition, a creature must actually have been declared as an attacker against the Leader. Putting a creature onto the battlefield already attacking does not count as declaring that attack.
Copying and turning face up
When an Identity turns face up, use its normal copiable values again while continuing to apply effects already affecting it.
A face-down Identity that copies another Identity still has the characteristics imposed by being face down. When it later turns face up, it shows the copied values. Apply the usual Magic copying rules together with these Identity rules.
Teams and opponents
Face-up Leaders and Guardians form the Leader team.
Face-up Assassins form the Assassin team.
Each Traitor forms a separate team and has no teammates, including other Traitors.
A player with a face-down Identity has no teammates and is an opponent of the other players until it is face up.
This distinction matters for effects referring to an opponent or teammate. Do not treat a hidden Guardian as a face-up teammate for targeting or card effects merely because you suspect their role.
Turns remain individual. Treachery does not grant shared turns, shared life totals, or shared mana.
Winning and losing
Normal Magic game-ending rules continue to apply, with these team conditions and exceptions:
A team loses when all of its players have lost.
The Leader team loses when all players controlling Leader Identities have lost, even if Guardians remain. This overrides an effect that would otherwise stop a Guardian from losing.
The Assassin team wins when all Leaders have lost and at least one Assassin Identity remains in the game.
A Traitor wins when every opponent has left, including every other Traitor.
If a player on a team wins, the entire team wins.
A Traitor therefore usually needs the Assassins eliminated before removing the Leader. Simply killing the Leader while an Assassin can claim the victory does not fulfill the Traitor's objective.
Leaving the game
Reveal all face-down Identities controlled by a departing player. The game remembers that player's last team using their last known Identity.
Apply normal multiplayer removal of that player's owned objects, with two Identity exceptions:
An ability already on the stack whose source is an Identity and whose owner leaves remains on the stack. Let the departing player resolve it if possible.
An Identity owned by the departing player but controlled by someone still in the game stays. Its remaining controller becomes its new owner.
At the end of the game, reveal every remaining face-down Identity.
Optional setups
Simple role cards
The source offers basic lands instead of custom Identities: Plains for Leader, Island for Guardian, Mountain for Assassin, and Swamp for Traitor. Use the chosen distribution and role objectives. This simplified option supplies roles without the custom cards' unveil effects; the land's ordinary text is not an Identity ability.
Backstab Rumble
Prepare exactly one Leader and make every other Identity a Traitor. Each Traitor still acts alone and must outlast every opponent, including other Traitors.
The source allows this option to be kept secret from players for surprise, overriding its usual public-distribution instruction. It changes the setup, not the Identity, unveil, or last-survivor procedures above.
Card restrictions and materials
Use the underlying format's banned/restricted list. The Treachery source additionally recommends avoiding Expropriate, Head Games, and Trade Secrets unless everyone agrees; that agreement cannot make a card legal in a base format that already bans it.

title: Pile o’ Magic Commander
text:
Pile o’ Magic Commander
Big Deck versions · Local rules: Commander version
This page includes the shared-Pile rules and the Commander changes together. The ordinary Pile o' Magic version has a different copy-limit rule.
Setup and Commander changes
Each player starts at 40 life and has a command zone.
Use singleton Pile construction instead of Singlesome: one copy per card name, except explicit card exceptions and ordinary basic-land exceptions.
Use the shared Pile and its minimum size below instead of separate 100-card libraries.
Choose one of the commander-selection procedures at the end of this page before play.
Ignore the requirement that the shared Pile's cards match an individual commander's color identity.
Once selected, commanders otherwise behave normally: command-zone movement, commander tax, and 21 combat damage from a single commander still apply.
Draw seven-card opening hands from the shared Pile, use normal multiplayer setup, and take individual turns.
Format Rule Changes
Unless otherwise noted, all normal Magic: The Gathering rules apply.
The Pile
Players all play out of a shared Library which is generally referred to as the Pile during construction or in format rules.
A pile may be formed in a few manners:
Messy Pile: Players all bring their own set of 45+ cards to shuffle into the Pile.
Themed Pile: A Pile is constructed in advance (collaboratively or by a host) which adheres to a central theme, MTG Set, mechanical archetype, etc.
Lands
Generally speaking, lands that only have mana abilities are not included in the Pile. Instead, we have included a classification of Heap Lands which is simply a list of Land cards Players will be able to retrieve from outside the game.
Once per turn, during their Upkeep, a player may place a card from their hand in the absolutely-removed-from-the-freaking-game-forever zone. That player then adds a Heap Land from outside the game to their hand. The chosen Heap Land must be able to produce mana of each color in the removed card’s Color Identity; it must not be able to produce mana of any additional colors.
This mechanic may be streamlined in practice to simply putting the card in a designated “land area” with the understanding that it now represents the specified land. Many players will prefer this over having a separate pile of lands outside the game.
Valid Heap Lands are defined below in the Pile Composition section.
Zones
Players share a Library and an absolutely-removed-from-the-freaking-game-forever zone. Other zones (graveyard, exile, etc) are not shared.
This may lead to interesting strategies around milling, recursion, and so on. Such unexpected effects are fine and shouldn’t be concerning unless they begin to lessen the fun for players.
Pile Composition
Card Count
For maximum madness, the traditional deck size is ~300 cards. However, Themed Piles may benefit from smaller card pools. The minimum Pile size is 45x(number of players).
Heap Lands
The following Land cards are considered valid Heap Lands which can be retrieved from outside the game in accordance with the rules.
Basic Lands: Plains, Island, Swamp, Mountain, Forest, Wastes
Dual-Color Lands
Generic: Meandering River, Submerged Boneyard, Cinder Barrens, Timber Gorge, Tranquil Expanse, Forsaken Sanctuary, Foul Orchard, Woodland Stream, Highland Lake, Stone Quarry
Dual-Types: Idyllic Beachfront, Contaminated Aquifer, Geothermal Bog, Wooded Ridgeline, Radiant Grove, Sunlit Marsh, Haunted Mire, Tangled Islet, Molten Tributary, Sacred Peaks
Tri-Color Lands: Seaside Citadel, Arcane Sanctum, Crumbling Necropolis, Savage Lands, Jungle Shrine, Nomad Outpost, Frontier Bivouac, Sandsteppe Citadel, Mystic Monastery, Opulent Palace
Five-Color Land: Transguild Promenade
Four-Color Lands? Unfortunately, there are no straightforward four-color lands. Feel free to make some up (I like these Gates by Reddit user TerryTags). Or maybe allow four color cards to retrieve a Transguild Promenade. Decide together. These cards aren’t very common– it won’t come up much.
Sleeves
When playing with a Messy Pile, should Players avoid sleeving their cards to prevent opponents gaining insight on the content of their hands? Should all Players re-sleeve their cards to one shared color/style?
In short: no. Players should still sleeve their cards (with unique sleeves!) so that ownership is easy to establish at the end of the game.
Will the sleeves potentially present information to your opponents? Yeah, sometimes. It is a consequence of the format, but not one that often impacts the fun.
Disallowed Cards
Tutors
Tutoring is generally against the “play what you find” spirit of Pile o’ Magic. They should be discouraged for the sole reason that they will take an inordinate amount of time to resolve. (The deck is enormous and players won’t know all the cards if you’ve built a Messy Pile*.)
This isn’t a true “ban” on the card type. Total bans would prevent funny cards like Booster Tutor which don’t have the same issues. Just consider carefully before including any tutors– will they truly add to the fun?
Addendum: For cards like Tempest Hawk you could consider just having a separate pile of fetchable Tempest Hawks set aside, though no formalized rules or considerations have been made for this concept. Talk to your group.
Rules Clarifications
The Absolutely-removed-from-the-freaking-game-forever Zone
Cards in the ARFTFGF Zone are outside “Outside The Game”- they cannot be played by cards like Wish. (https://markrosewater.tumblr.com/post/146325356493/i-get-that-a-card-removed-from-the-game-for)
Additionally, “Forever” only refers to the duration of the current game. (https://markrosewater.tumblr.com/post/50514158983/if-a-player-has-his-creature-hit-with-an-awol-can)
Other References
Four-Color Gates by Reddit User TerryTags
Four-Color Gates by Reddit User TerryTags
Source: A cycle of four-color lands by Reddit user TerryTags.
Commander selection
Let the Pile decide.
The first option we’ll examine is to find a Commander using the Pile. Prior to the game, each Player reveals cards from the top of the Pile until they reveal a Creature. That Creature becomes their Commander and is moved to the Command Zone. You may also limit this to the first Legendary Creature they reveal (or whatever restrictions you like).
The Creature revealed may not (likely will not) match the Color Identity of the entire deck, which is usually a requirement when building a Commander deck. For “Pile o’ Magic: Commander” we will ignore this requirement. During play, the Commander otherwise behaves as normal.
Bring your own.
Option number 2 is to just bring your own Commander! Each Player brings a 5-color Legendary Creature (separate from any cards being contributed to a Messy Pile) which will serve as their Commander.
Try to avoid bringing Commanders with tutor-like effects. They enable Players of Messy Piles to focus more on their own card contributions. The Players should be focused on playing into the unpredictable card pool of Pile o’ Magic.
Deal ‘em.
Now onto Option 3: each Player brings 3 Legendary Creatures which may serve as a Commander (disregard Color Identity). All of these creatures are shuffled together.
Each Player is dealt 3 random Commander candidates, they then choose the Commander they like (or think they can use) best. The remaining Commander candidates can be kept out of the game or shuffled into the Pile.
What specific Commanders are good for this format?
Fear not: I have opinions!
Tribals don’t work well because unless you’re playing a specific creature-type themed Pile, you won’t reliably be able to use tribal effects.
Commanders which tutor or search for specific categories are going to slow play tremendously and may suffer similar issues as tribals.
Commanders which generically enhance other cards, gain strength themselves, or get value out of mana or spells are going to work nicely. Whatever the Pile provides, you’ll utilize it!
Commanders in Pile o’ Magic


Commander
Status
Why
The Ur-Dragon
Bad
Tribal
Jodah, The Unifier
Bad
Search

Bad
A Tribal Search– oof.
Kenrith, the Returned King
Good

Omnath, Locus of All
Good
Value from mana

Good
Self-empowerment, mana generation

Local rules still needing decisions
The shared-library ownership, leaving-the-game, simultaneous-draw, mulligan, and Heap Land timing questions from ordinary Pile o' Magic remain unresolved here.
The Pile-selection method also needs a destination for revealed non-commander cards. The recorded selection procedure does not say whether they return to the Pile, go to its bottom, or are shuffled back. Decide this before selecting commanders; do not silently discard those cards.

Big Deck versions · Local rules: shared-library game
Pile o' Magic is the owner's formalization of Big Deck Magic. The complete recorded rules follow. For the Commander version, use Pile o' Magic Commander.
Setup
Prepare a Messy or Themed Pile using the construction rules below, plus the agreed Heap Lands or land-area markers. Use normal multiplayer setup, starting at 20 life and drawing seven cards unless the table chooses another underlying format. Draw from the shared Pile. Normal individual turns and normal Magic victory conditions apply unless changed below.
Format Rule Changes
Unless otherwise noted, all normal Magic: The Gathering rules apply.
The Pile
Players all play out of a shared Library which is generally referred to as the Pile during construction or in format rules.
A pile may be formed in a few manners:
Messy Pile: Players all bring their own set of 45+ cards to shuffle into the Pile.
Themed Pile: A Pile is constructed in advance (collaboratively or by a host) which adheres to a central theme, MTG Set, mechanical archetype, etc.
Lands
Generally speaking, lands that only have mana abilities are not included in the Pile. Instead, we have included a classification of Heap Lands which is simply a list of Land cards Players will be able to retrieve from outside the game.
Once per turn, during their Upkeep, a player may place a card from their hand in the absolutely-removed-from-the-freaking-game-forever zone. That player then adds a Heap Land from outside the game to their hand. The chosen Heap Land must be able to produce mana of each color in the removed card’s Color Identity; it must not be able to produce mana of any additional colors.
This mechanic may be streamlined in practice to simply putting the card in a designated “land area” with the understanding that it now represents the specified land. Many players will prefer this over having a separate pile of lands outside the game.
Valid Heap Lands are defined below in the Pile Composition section.
Zones
Players share a Library and an absolutely-removed-from-the-freaking-game-forever zone. Other zones (graveyard, exile, etc) are not shared.
This may lead to interesting strategies around milling, recursion, and so on. Such unexpected effects are fine and shouldn’t be concerning unless they begin to lessen the fun for players.

Copy limits: Singlesome
Part of the fun of Pile o’ Magic is the element of discovery– and of unique games. In general, you should try to avoid including multiple copies of cards.
Of course, when making a Messy Pile*, you could end up with duplicates even if players avoid bringing them. Additionally, some cards only make sense to include with duplicates (S.N.O.T.)
The maximum copies of a single card allowed in the Pile is 4x(number of Players). Except for the exceptions, of course (Rat Colony, Hare Apparent).
Local rules still needing decisions
The recorded design leaves these interactions for a future ruling:
Who owns a card drawn from the shared library for in-game ownership effects, and what happens when a contributor leaves the game.
The order of simultaneous draws from the Pile and handling of mulligans involving the same library.
Whether exchanging a card for a Heap Land is a special action or an ability, and its exact timing within upkeep.
The chosen four-color Heap Land option.
The standard last-player-standing and ordinary Magic loss conditions apply unless the group explicitly chooses otherwise. Any new box must state its answers to the shared-library questions rather than assume another Big Deck format's rules.

title: Creature Feature Rules
text:
Creature Feature Rules
Creature Feature parent page · Local rules: Pegasus Loft
Creature Feature is a local Pegasus Loft constructed format that uses normal Magic gameplay, but adds deck-building pressure around creature density and shared creature types.
Core Rules
Decks have a 60-card minimum.
At least half of the deck must be creature cards, rounded up.
At least two thirds of the creature cards in the deck must share a creature type, rounded up.
Games are played as normal Magic unless the event organizer announces an additional house rule.
Use normal constructed deck-building rules unless the event organizer announces otherwise.
Creature Type Requirement
Choose one creature type as the deck's featured type. A creature card counts toward the shared-type requirement if its Oracle creature types include the featured type.
For example:
A 60-card deck needs at least 30 creature cards.
If that deck has 30 creature cards, at least 20 of those creatures must share the featured type.
If that deck has 31 creature cards, at least 21 of those creatures must share the featured type.
Creatures with multiple creature types can count for any type they have. Changelings count as having every creature type unless the event organizer has separately banned or restricted that interaction.
Temporary Type Bans
When a creature type wins a Creature Feature tournament, that creature type should be temporarily banned for the next four weeks.
The goal is to keep dominant types from repeating every event, especially creature types with deep tribal support such as Eldrazi or Sliver. After the temporary ban expires, the type becomes legal again unless it wins another event.
Negative Creature-Type Hate
Cards that negatively target creature types are banned.
This includes cards whose main purpose is to punish, remove, shrink, prevent, or otherwise disadvantage a named creature type. Color hate, mana-value hate, graveyard hate, artifact hate, and other non-type-specific answers are still legal unless they are banned by another rule.
Use this as the practical test: if the card asks a player to choose or name a creature type and then harms that type or gives protection from that type, it should not be played in Creature Feature.
Event Notes
Keep a visible list of currently banned creature types and the date each ban expires.
Record the winning featured type after each event.
If a winning deck uses multiple creature types heavily, ban the type that satisfied the two-thirds requirement.
If the event uses sideboards, the deck should still satisfy the creature-count and shared-type requirements after sideboarding.
Before an event
The organizer must announce the permitted card pool, any additional house rules, whether sideboards are used, and the current temporary type bans. The existing rules do not select a sanctioned constructed format's legality list automatically.
A temporary type ban needs a clear event interpretation: does it prohibit choosing that featured type, or prohibit every card with that type? This matters especially for changelings. That decision has not been recorded in the local rules.
Setup, play, and victory
After checking deck legality, play normal Magic using the event's announced structure. For an ordinary two-player constructed game, each player starts at 20 life, draws seven, uses normal mulligans, and the starting player skips their first draw. Normal turn structure, combat, and win/loss conditions apply. Multiplayer events use normal multiplayer setup instead.
No special victory condition is added by Creature Feature. After each event, record the winner's declared featured type and the expiration of its four-week ban.
Provenance
These are the local Pegasus Loft rules recorded in this repository. They are not an official Wizards format or a rule imported from another creature-type format.

title: Cube
text:
Cube
All formats
Rulesets
Booster-draft Cube: full play rules, including pack preparation, every draft round, deck construction, and game setup.
The construction styles below describe the card pool. Other draft methods mentioned here need separate rules pages before they can be used as self-contained instructions.
The Cube
Cube is a Limited format built from a curated pool of Magic cards. Instead of opening retail booster packs, players draft from custom "packs" made from the cube owner's card pool, then build decks from the cards they drafted. Wizards describes Cube as being like Booster Draft, but with cards pulled from across Magic's history. Source: Arena Powered Cube Draft.
The cube itself is not a deck. It is the reusable draft environment.
Basic Concept
A cube is usually a few hundred cards selected by its designer. The designer chooses the themes, power level, colors, archetypes, and constraints. Before a draft, the cube is randomized and divided into draft packs, usually fifteen cards each. Players draft those packs like a normal Booster Draft, build decks, play matches, and return the cards to the cube afterward. Source: Power, Cubed.
Most cubes are singleton, meaning they include only one copy of each non-basic-land card. That is common, but not required. Some cubes use duplicates for balance, theme, or to support specific archetypes. Wizards' cube articles describe singleton as typical for many cubes, while also noting variations in cube size, restriction, and structure. Sources: Power, Cubed, Building Your First Cube.
Why Build A Cube?
Cube lets a group draft the kind of Magic environment they want on demand. It can feel like a greatest-hits Limited format, a nostalgia set, a custom expansion, a high-powered Vintage draft, a peasant environment, a set cube, a Commander draft box, or something much stranger.
For game-night purposes, cube is useful because the host can prepare the entire experience in advance:
The card pool.
The draft structure.
The land station.
The number of players supported.
The intended power level.
Any house rules or special draft rules.
Common Cube Types
Powered Cube: High-powered cards, often including extremely efficient spells and fast mana.
Unpowered Cube: Strong cards, but without the most explosive power outliers.
Peasant Cube: Only commons and uncommons.
Pauper Cube: Only commons.
Set Cube: Recreates the feel of drafting a specific Magic set, often with duplicates.
Theme Cube: Built around a plane, mechanic, creature type, color restriction, story, or custom design goal.
Commander Cube: Drafted for multiplayer Commander-style games, usually with special commander selection rules.
Drafting And Building
The default cube experience mirrors Booster Draft:
Each player drafts three packs.
Packs are often fifteen cards.
Players build minimum forty-card decks.
Basic lands are supplied separately.
That default is flexible. Smaller groups might draft more packs, use sealed pools, grid draft, Winston draft, rotisserie draft, or other draft variants. A cube can support whatever draft method the owner wants. Wizards' cube guidance emphasizes that cube size and structure are design choices rather than one fixed template. Source: Building Your First Cube.
Boxed-Set Notes
For reusable draft-pack containers, see Dragon Shield Cube Shells and decorative Cubeamajigs in Useful Products & Tools, including purchase links, capacity, and quantities for an eight-player draft.
A cube box should probably include:
The cube card pool.
Basic lands or a land station.
Draft instructions.
Player-count guidance.
Any custom rules or archetype notes.
Tokens, counters, and helper cards used by the cube.
A changelog if the cube evolves over time.
References
Building Your First Cube
Power, Cubed
Arena Powered Cube Draft

title: Booster-Draft Cube
text:
Booster-Draft Cube
Cube parent page · Rules: ordinary booster drafting with a reusable card pool
Players and materials
Prepare a curated cube, an adequate supply of basic lands, and tokens or counters for its cards. Eight players is a common draft size; the pool needs at least 45 cards per player for the three-pack, fifteen-card setup below.
A cube's theme, rarity restrictions, power level, and choice to use duplicates are construction decisions. They do not change the draft procedure unless the owner explicitly adds a rule.
Prepare the draft
Choose the cube list and any announced special rules.
Randomize its cards and make three fifteen-card packs for each player.
Keep unused cube cards outside the draft.
Seat players in a circle and give each player their three packs.
Everyone opens only the first pack.
The owner may use deliberately seeded packs, but must specify that construction method. It is not part of the randomized default.
Draft pack one
Look privately at the cards in the current pack.
Choose one card and place it face down in your drafted pool.
Pass the remaining cards to the player on your left.
Receive the next pack from your right and repeat.
Continue until every card from the first round of packs has been selected.
Keep selections separate from packs being passed so cards cannot be accidentally returned to a pack.
Draft packs two and three
Open pack two when everyone has finished the first round. Repeat the same one-card-per-pick procedure, but pass to the right.
For pack three, pass to the left again.
Each player finishes with 45 drafted cards. A procedure that takes two cards at a time, drafts commanders separately, or passes in a different pattern is a separate variant and must be announced.
Build decks
Build a deck of at least 40 cards from your drafted pool.
Add ordinary basic lands from the land supply as needed.
You may play any number of copies of a card you actually drafted; the constructed four-copy limit does not apply.
Your undrafted remainder is not available. Your drafted cards that are not in the main deck form your sideboard.
You may change the deck using that sideboard and the supplied basic lands between games, keeping at least 40 cards.
Drafting a legendary creature does not automatically turn this into Commander. This ruleset does not create a command zone, color-identity restriction, commander tax, or commander-damage condition.
Play games
Choose pairings and a match structure before play. In normal two-player games, each player starts at 20 life, draws seven cards, and uses normal mulligans. Determine who chooses to play or draw normally; the player taking the first turn skips their first draw step.
Play ordinary Magic turns and combat with normal victory and loss conditions. If the group wants multiplayer free-for-all matches instead, announce that structure and use its normal multiplayer setup.
Reset the cube
At the end of play, return every drafted card to the cube, separate the borrowed basic lands, and check that tokens and other components have been collected. The cube is reusable; drafting does not transfer ownership of its cards.
Other cube structures
Powered, unpowered, peasant, pauper, set, and theme cubes can all use this procedure. Commander Cube, Winston draft, grid draft, sealed pools, and rotisserie draft require their own additional procedures; mentioning those possibilities is not a complete ruleset for them.
Sources: Wizards' Booster Draft rules, Building Your First Cube, and Power, Cubed.

Author: Peter Knudson Published: October 26, 2011
This follow-up article treats Horde Magic as an open-source casual format. It gathers early community feedback, discusses scaling and planeswalkers, introduces preconstructed Survivor decks, shares alternate Horde deck ideas, and proposes a first banned list.
Main Design Point
The article argues that the format should be easy to change. If the Zombie Horde is too easy or too hard, the first lever should usually be the Horde deck itself rather than making the rules more complicated.
Scaling Problems
Some players found the Horde too easy with more Survivors. The article suggests reducing setup turns for 3-4 player games from three turns to two.
The author prefers preserving the simple rules engine and increasing difficulty through card selection:
Remove weak Horde cards.
Add more threatening non-token cards.
Include better sweepers or reset effects.
Tune the Horde deck to the Survivor decks being used.
Suggested Horde Additions
Card
Reason
Noxious Ghoul
Flavorful Zombie sweeper.
All Is Dust
Broad reset effect that punishes overbuilt defenses.
Smallpox
Early disruption; sacrifice choices can be handled simply.
Mnemonic Nexus
Can refill the Horde late and create a surprise reset.
Vulturous Zombie
Adds a large flying threat.
Living Death
Flavorful, swingy board reset.
Planeswalker Rule
The original article did not handle planeswalkers cleanly.
The proposed solution:
If Survivors control one or more planeswalkers, flip a coin at the beginning of Horde combat.
On heads, the Horde randomly allocates attackers to planeswalkers.
Allocate one Zombie per point of loyalty for each planeswalker, starting in random planeswalker order if there are multiple.
This is not elegant, but it gives planeswalkers risk without making the Horde too decision-heavy.
Preconstructed Survivor Decks
The article suggests building fixed Survivor Commander decks designed to fight the Horde. These could work like party roles: Fighter, Cleric, Wizard, and so on.
The included example is a green-white Survivor deck by @mtgcolorpie, with Tolsimir Wolfblood as commander. The article likes it because it is thematic, not overpowered, and full of defensive / soldier-flavored cards.
Alternate Horde Deck Ideas
The article collects several community Horde concepts.
Sliver Horde
Credit: @wobbles
The Sliver Horde uses small Slivers that become more dangerous as lords accumulate. The article notes that Sliver Overlord could be placed at the bottom of the deck to create an end-boss feeling.
Cat Horde
Credit: d0su from MTG Salvation
Cat tokens are close to Zombie tokens in baseline stats, which makes them easier to adapt. The deck mixes mediocre cats, larger threats, and multicolor finishers.
Merfolk Horde
Credit: @Bassiuz
The Merfolk Horde uses smaller tokens but leans on lords and disruptive blue-white effects. The article calls out cards such as Hysterical Blindness, Summon the School, and Balance as examples of collection finds that can become Horde cards.
