Horde Magic Wiki Summary — Source Notes
For the play procedure, open the dedicated rules page. These notes preserve source context and historical discussion.
Source: https://mtg.fandom.com/wiki/Horde_Magic#Rules_for_The_Horde
This source summarizes Horde Magic as a casual multiplayer format where all players work together against an automated Horde deck.
Format Snapshot
Field
Value
DCI sanctioned
No
Paper
No official sanctioning
Magic Online
No
Magic Arena
No
Type
Constructed casual variant
Multiplayer
Yes
Format Goals
Spirit
Horde Magic is casual and social. If a rule or card interaction makes the game less fun, the table should agree on a practical fix. Cycling or replacing problematic cards is a common solution.
Flavor
The original theme was a zombie apocalypse. The automated rules fit zombies well because the Horde should make as few choices as possible. Other thematic Hordes can work as long as the deck remains flavorful and functional.
Participants
Horde Magic has two sides:
The Horde: An automated deck.
The Survivors: The human players acting cooperatively.
Win Conditions
The Horde wins if:
The Survivors' shared life total is reduced to 0 or less.
The Survivors win if:
The Horde has no cards in its library.
The Horde has no cards in hand.
The Horde controls no creatures.
Rules For The Horde
The Horde has no player and pilots itself.
Any choice the Horde must make should be made as randomly as possible.
The Horde has infinite mana at all times.
At the start of the Horde's turn, reveal cards from the top of its library until a non-token card is revealed.
Cast all revealed tokens, then cast the revealed non-token card.
If applicable, the Horde also casts cards from its graveyard and hand.
All Horde creatures have haste and must attack each turn if able.
The Horde has no life total.
Damage dealt to the Horde, or life loss inflicted on the Horde, causes it to mill that many cards instead.
Lifelink still works for players, but the Horde cannot "unmill" cards.
Rules For The Survivors
The Survivors take three setup turns before the Horde gets its first turn.
After setup, turns alternate normally.
The Survivors are a team and take their turns simultaneously, similar to Two-Headed Giant.

Horde Magic 2.0: Introducing The Raid — Source Notes
For the play procedure, open the dedicated rules page. These notes preserve source context and historical discussion.
Source: https://www.quietspeculation.com/2013/02/horde-magic-2-0-introducing-the-raid/
Author: Peter Knudson Published: February 18, 2013
This article revisits Horde Magic and proposes Raid, a staged variant where the Horde deck becomes more like a roleplaying quest or dungeon.
Premise
The article frames Horde Magic as a story generator. A good Horde deck should not just be a pile of enemy cards; it should explain what the Survivors are fighting, why the battle matters, and what kind of memorable moments the table is trying to create.
Raid pushes this further by letting the Horde designer act a bit like a dungeon master.
Raid Rules
Raid uses normal Horde Magic as its base, with three major changes:
The Horde deck is semi-ordered before play.
Cards inside each quest or stage are randomized, but the stages occur in a set order.
Artifacts revealed by the Horde do not count as non-token cards; they become loot for the Survivors.
Survivors cannot attack the Horde deck directly.
Because Survivors cannot mill the Horde by attacking, Raid is more defensive and scenario-driven.
Why Semi-Order The Deck?
The deck order lets the scenario tell a story. Survivors can fight through one stage, then another, then a boss or finale.
Within each stage, the cards can still be randomized so the game does not play out exactly the same way every time.
Example: The Dragonborn
The article's first Raid example is inspired by Skyrim. The Survivors fight through wilderness creatures, soldiers, vampires, undead, dragons, and a final boss.
Stage Order
Green cards and tokens.
First Dragon Boss.
White cards and tokens.
Second Dragon Boss.
Black cards and tokens.
Red cards and Zombie tokens.
Final Boss.
Story Shape
The Survivors are trapped in hostile wilderness, then move through escalating conflicts before confronting a world-ending dragon threat.
The author notes that this list may favor the Survivors and suggests possible fixes such as adding a reset rule after each stage or adding more sweepers.
Example: Rat Horde
The second example uses Gatecrash-era Rat support.
The setup is a city overrun by rats and a criminal syndicate. Survivors must exterminate the infestation before disease overtakes the city.
Rat Horde Design Notes
Rat tokens are small, so the deck uses anthem-like effects to scale over time.
Poison counters act as a doom clock.
If ten poison counters are revealed, the Survivors lose.
Sorin emblems are used like token flips: they continue the reveal chain and permanently buff the rats.
Bad Moon appears as an additional scaling hedge.
Other Horde Deck Ideas
The article closes with more thematic Horde prompts:
Eldrazi
Elementals
Angels
Demons
Dragons
Assassins
Pirates
Rebels
Soldiers
Saprolings
Goblins
Spirits
Beasts
Dinosaurs
Takeaways For Game-Night Boxes
Raid is especially relevant to boxed game nights because it supports scenario packaging:
A staged enemy deck.
Boss cards or boss packets.
Loot cards.
Scenario sheets.
Difficulty adjustments between stages.
A campaign structure where the table fights multiple Raids in sequence.
Raid also makes Horde more self-contained. If the box includes Survivor decks, the host can tune both sides into a fixed cooperative experience.

HordeMagic.com EDH-Style Variant — Source Notes
For the play procedure, open the dedicated rules page. These notes preserve source context and historical discussion.
Source: https://hordemagic.com/
This source presents a modern EDH-style Horde Magic variant inspired by Peter Knudson's original Horde Magic rules.
Related Source Links
Original Horde Magic article: https://www.quietspeculation.com/2011/09/horde-magic-a-new-way-to-play-magic-and-survive-zombie-invasions/
Horde Magic follow-up: https://www.quietspeculation.com/2011/10/horde-magic-an-open-source-project/
MTG Wiki rules summary: https://mtg.fandom.com/wiki/Horde_Magic#Rules_for_The_Horde
Premise
Horde Magic is a cooperative Magic format where one to four players fight an automated enemy deck. This version assumes players use EDH decks against a large Horde library.
Player Setup
Each player chooses an EDH deck.
Players take three setup turns before the Horde takes its first turn, unless the scenario says otherwise.
The setup turns let players establish a minimal board before the Horde begins producing waves.
Horde Gameplay
The Horde has a roughly 300-card library.
The Horde has infinite mana for casting costs and activation costs.
The Horde casts spells in waves.
Cards are cast from the top of the Horde library until the wave ends.
The Horde does not have a hand.
If the Horde would draw a card, it puts that card directly into play instead.
If a Horde-owned permanent would return to the Horde's hand, put it on top of the Horde library instead.
If the Horde is instructed to discard, it may put the top card of its library into its graveyard.
Creature Rules
Horde creatures have haste.
Horde creatures are goaded unless otherwise stated.
Only Horde creatures with defender can block.
Card-triggered abilities happen immediately.
Activated abilities follow summoning sickness.
Activated abilities happen during the post-combat main phase.
A permanent with an activated ability can activate that ability only once per turn.
Waves
The Horde plays one wave per turn by default.
Optional: Increase wave count based on the number of players.
Optional: Use a repeating wave count pattern such as 1, 2, 3, 2, 1, 2, 3, 2, 1.
Waves end when an uncommon, rare, or mythic card enters the battlefield.
Player Team Rules
One to four human players can battle the Horde.
Human players act as a single team, taking turns and phases in unison.
The Horde is also treated as a player.
Player life totals are combined.

Each player beyond the first reduces the starting shared life total by 15.
Damage And Life
Damage dealt to the Horde mills that many cards from the Horde library.
Optional recommended rule: If a legendary creature is milled this way, it enters the battlefield and then phases out instead.
Lifegain for the Horde has no effect.
Optional: Horde lifegain may put cards from the Horde graveyard on the bottom of the Horde library.
Damage dealt to the players reduces the shared life total.
Lifegain by the players increases the shared life total.
"Each Player" And "Each Opponent"
Effects that refer to each player trigger for each player.
Effects that refer to each opponent trigger only once.
Horde Decisions
When the Horde must make a decision, make the decision in the Horde's best interest. The source emphasizes honesty: the challenge is the fun.
Win Conditions
The players win if:
The Horde library is empty.
The Horde battlefield is empty.
The Horde wins if:
The players have no life.
The players have no cards to draw.
The players reach the poison limit.
Cards with alternate win conditions, such as "you win the game" text, are not legal.
Ban Philosophy
The ban list is meant to prevent cards that make the Horde nonfunctional or mathematically trivial to beat. Permanents with one-shot effects are more acceptable than static effects that permanently shut down the Horde.
Cards are suspect if they:
Make Horde creatures enter tapped.
Kill Horde creatures as they enter.
Mill the Horde on enter-the-battlefield or graveyard triggers.
Gain life based on the cumulative power of attacks.
Make the matchup mathematically too easy.

text:
Horde Magic: A New Way To Play Magic And Survive Zombie Invasions — Source Notes
For the play procedure, open the dedicated rules page. These notes preserve source context and historical discussion.
Source: https://www.quietspeculation.com/2011/09/horde-magic-a-new-way-to-play-magic-and-survive-zombie-invasions/
Author: Peter Knudson Published: September 29, 2011
This is the original Horde Magic article. It introduces the format as a cooperative Magic variant where players team up against an automated Zombie Horde deck.
Premise
Horde Magic is framed as "Left 4 Dead" Magic: the players are Survivors trying to outlast a zombie apocalypse.
The Horde has no pilot, no hand, and no life total. It attacks relentlessly. The players win by surviving long enough to exhaust the Horde deck and clear the battlefield.
Basic Setup
Each Survivor uses a Commander deck, though the article notes that other Magic decks can work.
One to four Survivors play cooperatively.
Survivors share a life total.
The Horde deck starts with no hand and no permanents.
Survivors take three setup turns before the Horde takes its first turn.
After setup, the Survivors and Horde alternate turns.
Horde Deck Size By Player Count
Survivors
Horde Deck Size
1
45 cards
2
60 cards
3
75 cards
4
100 cards
The article's method is to build a 100-card Horde deck, then randomly remove cards for smaller player counts.
Survivor Rules
Survivors act like a team.
Survivors take their turns simultaneously.
Survivors attack and block as a team.
The shared life total is 20 life per player.
Horde Turn
On each Horde turn:
Reveal the top card of the Horde library.
If it is a Zombie token, keep revealing cards.
Stop when a non-token card is revealed.
Cast all revealed tokens.
Cast the revealed non-token card last.
Move to combat.
All Zombies have haste and must attack each turn if able.
Damaging The Horde
The Horde has no life total. For each point of damage dealt to the Horde, mill one card from the top of the Horde library.
The Survivors win when:
The Horde library is empty.
The Horde controls no Zombies.
The Horde wins when:
The Survivors' shared life total reaches 0.
Rules Notes
The Horde deck should avoid cards that require decisions.
If the Horde must make a choice, make the choice randomly.
Horde tokens and spells use the stack and can be responded to.
The Horde has infinite mana, so effects like Propaganda and Mana Leak do not function as normal answers.
If a permanent is returned to the Horde's hand, it is cast again during the Horde's next main phase.
If something does not work cleanly, the table should choose the fairest execution or cycle the problematic card.

Design Notes
The article discusses a few early design choices:
The deck needs variance, but dice-based variance felt inelegant.
Non-token cards create tension because players do not know whether the next reveal is harmless or devastating.
Sweepers and reset effects pressure Survivors to attack the Horde instead of turtling forever.
Scaling is difficult because every additional Survivor adds more draw steps, mana development, and actions.
Persistent effects such as Bad Moon help the Horde scale as the game goes longer.
Future Idea: Survivor Decks
The editor's note suggests preconstructed Survivor decks designed and balanced against the Horde. This would make the format more plug-and-play for players without Commander decks and could create class-like roles for the Survivor team.

Survivors shuffle their decks, prepare any commanders, draw their opening hands, and use normal mulligans.
Set the survivor team's shared life total to 20 per player.
Survivors take three shared turns before the Horde takes its first turn.
Survivor turns and resources
Survivors take their phases and steps together. Each player draws from their own library, controls their own permanents, uses their own mana, and makes their own land play. They coordinate attacks and blocks.
Damage, life loss, and life gain affecting the survivors change their shared life total. The source's special shared-life setup replaces the usual individual Commander starting life.
The Horde's turn
After the setup turns, alternate a Horde turn with a shared survivor turn.
Reveal the top card of the Horde library.
If it is a Zombie token, continue revealing.
Stop at the first non-token card, or when the library runs out.
Cast the revealed tokens, then cast the revealed non-token card last if there is one.
Proceed to combat. Horde Zombies have haste and must attack if able.
The Horde's spells use the stack and players can respond, including countering them. Having infinite mana does not mean they bypass the stack.
The Horde attacks the survivor team. Survivors can block together for the team. Horde Zombies cannot block, so attacking the Horde does not require getting past its Zombies.
Horde mana, choices, and cards
The Horde has unlimited mana for costs. Mana taxes such as Propaganda or Mana Leak do not stop it by requiring a payment it cannot afford. Non-mana costs still require whatever the card instructs.
Build the Horde to minimize choices. When an effect nevertheless requires a choice, make it as randomly as possible among legal options.
A permanent returned to the Horde's hand is cast again during its next main phase. The Horde starts with no hand; that does not erase the original rule for cards returned to its hand.
When a card interaction does not function in this automated format, the original source asks the group to choose a fair handling or cycle the problematic card. Agree the exact replacement procedure if using that escape hatch; the source does not define its cycling cost or timing.
Damaging and defeating the Horde
The Horde has no life total. Each point of damage dealt to it puts one card from the top of its library into its graveyard. Survivors may attack it to reduce future waves.
The survivors win when the Horde library is empty and no Horde Zombies remain on the battlefield. An empty library alone is not victory while Zombies remain.
The Horde wins when the survivor team's shared life reaches zero or less.
Source limitations and other versions
The original article does not specify a complete set of special rules for poison, alternate-win cards, or every modern card type. It also does not have the follow-up's planeswalker attack procedure. Record additional decisions before using interactions that need them.
For a specific planeswalker procedure and the 2011 ban list, choose the Open Source version. For a different life system and rarity-based waves, choose HordeMagic.com.

Players, decks, and setup
Use one to four human players, each with an EDH deck, against a Horde library of approximately 300 cards. The Horde has no pilot and no hand. Prepare tokens and any scenario-specific counters.

Prepare the survivor decks and command zones and take normal opening hands and mulligans. Shuffle the Horde unless a specific scenario instructs otherwise. The survivors take three shared turns before the Horde's first turn.
Shared survivor turns
Survivors act together through untap, phases, combat, and end step. Their life total is shared. They still operate their own decks and cards.
Damage or life loss to a survivor reduces the shared total; life gain increases it. The Horde counts as a player.
The source distinguishes these wordings:
An effect referring to each player applies for each human player.
An effect referring to each opponent applies once for the survivor group.
When the Horde attacks, the survivor group is considered one player for that attack. The source explicitly allows the survivors' abilities that trigger when they are attacked to trigger.
Horde turn and waves
After setup, alternate survivor and Horde turns. By default, the Horde plays one wave per turn.
Cast cards from the top of the Horde library, paying mana costs with its unlimited mana.
Continue until an uncommon, rare, or mythic card is cast.
That cast ends the wave. The current source uses casting, not entering the battlefield, as the stopping condition.
Move to combat.
During the post-combat main phase, use eligible activated abilities subject to the limits below.
Agree how the physical Horde list identifies a card's rarity; different printings can have different rarities.
Horde creatures and abilities
Horde creatures have haste and are goaded unless otherwise stated, such as by defender.
Only Horde creatures with defender may block.
The Horde has infinite mana for casting and activation costs.
The source applies summoning sickness to card-activated abilities and places their use in the post-combat main phase.
A permanent may have an activated ability activated only once per turn under this house rule.
The source calls for card-triggered abilities to happen immediately.
The source's broad wording about summoning sickness and “immediately” is not a full replacement for Magic's timing rules. If a chosen card requires a finer ruling about an untapped permanent, an ability without a tap cost, or a trigger on the stack, record that interpretation before using it.
Hand, draw, discard, and bounce
The Horde does not maintain a hand.
If it would draw a card, take that card and immediately cast it.
If a Horde-owned permanent would return to its hand, put it on top of the Horde library instead.
When offered a discard, the Horde may put the top card of its library into its graveyard.
Do not use Classic Horde's “recast from hand next main phase” rule in this version.
Damage, life gain, and choices
Each point of damage to the Horde mills a card from its library. The Horde has no ordinary life total and normally receives no benefit from life gain.
When the Horde must make a choice, choose in the Horde's best interest. This includes choosing targets. It is not the random-choice rule from Classic Horde.
Additional published interpretations
Exotic Orchard and Fellwar Stone: the source recommends letting these produce any color, even though the Horde has no lands.
Attack prevention: ignore static card rules that would prevent the Horde's creatures from attacking, including entering tapped or being unable to attack. Targeted effects, activated effects, and stun counters remain usable.
Monarch: the source assigns monarchy to the survivor group, but only one survivor draws its card. The group chooses the player who needs the draw.
These are this version's special interpretations, not universal Magic or Horde rules.
Victory and defeat
The survivors win only when both the Horde library and its battlefield are empty.
The Horde wins when the survivors run out of life, cannot draw, or reach the poison limit. Cards with alternate winning abilities, including “you win the game” effects, are not legal in this version.
The current source does not give a numerical poison threshold or fully specify whether a single survivor's empty library defeats the entire group. Choose those details before playing decks that can invoke them.
Optional modules
Choose modules before play and record the choice for a boxed set.
More waves
Increase the wave count for larger groups, or use the suggested repeating progression 1, 2, 3, 2, 1, 2, 3, 2, 1. A scenario using this should specify whether and how it repeats beyond the written sequence.
Legendary bosses
The source recommends roughly seven legendary creatures as bosses. With its optional damage-mill rule, when such a creature would go to the graveyard from damage milling, it enters the battlefield instead, triggers its enter-the-battlefield abilities, and then immediately phases out. It later phases in under normal phasing rules.
Horde life gain
Instead of ignoring Horde life gain, the group may put cards from its graveyard on the bottom of its library. The source does not specify the selection order or conversion rate, so a box adopting this module must provide those details.
Historical restrictions
The repository's older source notes preserve a ban list and two banned combinations. Those are retained as reference material; do not silently combine that older list with the current page's attack-prevention interpretation.

Horde Raid
Horde versions · Draft scenario framework: Peter Knudson's 2013 Raid variant
Raid uses the original Horde game with an ordered enemy deck, artifact loot, and a prohibition on survivor attacks against the Horde. The original article calls it a work in progress. Its actual procedures are below, followed by the scenario decisions the article leaves open.
Players and materials
Use one to four survivors with Commander decks or other agreed survivor decks. Prepare an enemy deck divided into named quest or stage packets, any boss cards, artifact loot, and the required tokens and counters.
Choose and record the scenario before play. Do not randomly cut a staged deck down using a Classic Horde player-count table without specifying how the cut preserves required stages and bosses.
Setup
Put the scenario's stage packets in their required order.
Randomize the cards within each stage, while preserving any specifically positioned boss cards.
Stack the stages so the first stage is drawn first. Do not shuffle the combined library.
Prepare survivor libraries and commanders, draw opening hands, and take normal mulligans.
Unless the scenario changes the original Horde setup, use 20 shared life per survivor and three shared setup turns.
The Horde begins with no hand or permanents. After the setup turns, alternate Horde and survivor turns.
Survivor turns and combat
Survivors take their turns together, with individual libraries, hands, mana, and land plays. They share life and defend together against Horde attacks.
Survivors cannot attack the Horde. This is the Raid replacement for Classic Horde's direct offensive combat. The article does not automatically prohibit every noncombat damage or mill effect; a scenario that wants that additional restriction must state it.
Revealing a wave and finding loot
Reveal the next card from the staged Horde library.
If it is a creature token, add it to the wave and keep revealing.
If it is an artifact, treat it as survivor loot. It does not count as the non-token card that ends the wave, so continue revealing.
Stop on the first other non-token card, or when the library runs out.
Cast the revealed enemy tokens and then the wave's non-token spell, using the normal Horde stack procedure.
Give artifact loot to the survivors using the scenario's declared allocation and timing rule.
The article identifies artifacts as loot but does not specify who receives them, whether they enter immediately or go to a hand, or how equipment is assigned. Those details must be supplied by a completed Raid box.
Horde combat and effects
Horde creatures have haste and attack the survivors when able. Survivors can block together. Use the original Horde's unlimited mana and random choices among legal options.
Horde spells and abilities can be responded to. A card returned to the Horde's hand can be cast on its next main phase under the original rule. The scenario must state any replacement for these procedures.
Noncombat damage to the Horde still mills one card per point under the inherited rules unless the scenario explicitly changes it. The ban on attacking does not itself define how a milled boss should be handled.
Stages, victory, and defeat
The stage order creates the sequence of encounters. The source does not add an automatic battlefield reset or heal between stages. If a scenario uses either, its rules must give the exact trigger and effect.
The inherited Horde objective is to exhaust the enemy deck and defeat its remaining creatures while preserving the survivors' shared life. The Horde wins when shared survivor life reaches zero or less. A scenario may replace this with a boss objective or another loss condition, but must write it out.
Published example: The Dragonborn
The article uses this ordered scenario:
Green cards and tokens.
First dragon boss.
White cards and tokens.
Second dragon boss.
Black cards and tokens.
Red cards and Zombie tokens.
Final boss.
Randomize within the listed groups. The author suggests a stage reset or additional sweepers as possible future tuning, not as finalized rules.
Published Rat Horde scenario additions
The same article gives another Horde deck example with two specific additions. They are not universal Raid rules:
When a poison-counter card is revealed, add it to the scenario's poison total. At ten such counters, the survivors lose.
Treat a Sorin emblem card as a token flip: it continues the reveal sequence and provides the emblem's continuing creature bonus.
Use the example's actual cards and a declared scenario setup if adopting those modules.
Decisions required for a complete Raid box
Exact enemy, boss, and survivor decklists and supported player counts.
Loot ownership, placement, allocation, and timing.
Whether a wave may reveal through a stage boundary and how stage transitions are announced.
Handling of bosses that are milled, exiled, or otherwise skipped.
Any between-stage reset or recovery procedure.
Exact scenario victory conditions and additional failure conditions.
Source: Horde Magic 2.0: Introducing the Raid, Peter Knudson, February 18, 2013. Archived scenario notes.

text:
Horde: Archived Wiki Version
Horde versions · Rules: wiki snapshot preserved in this repository
This page gives the procedures recorded in the repository's wiki notes. It is a distinct source version, not a claim that every Horde group uses these rules or that the snapshot matches the current wiki.
Players and materials
Use one to four survivors and an automated Horde. Survivors bring their own decks, normally Commander decks. A typical Horde has 100 cards: approximately 60 creature-token cards and 40 ordinary cards, selected to avoid decisions and suit the Horde's theme.
Prepare the tokens, counters, and shared life tracker needed by those decks.
Setup
Shuffle survivor decks and the Horde. Prepare commanders where applicable.
Survivors draw opening hands and take normal mulligans.
Start the survivor team at 20 life per player, combined into one shared total.
Survivors take three shared setup turns before the Horde's first turn.
After setup, alternate survivor and Horde turns.
The snapshot describes random removal of Horde cards as a difficulty option, but does not supply the original article's exact player-count table. If using that option, record how many cards are set aside.
Survivor turns
Survivors take their phases and steps simultaneously, similar to shared-team-turn Magic. They coordinate attacks and blocks as a team. Each player uses their own cards and resources; damage and life changes affect the shared total.
Horde turns
At the start of the Horde's turn, reveal cards until reaching a non-token card or exhausting the library.
Cast the revealed token cards first, then the non-token card if there is one.
The Horde also casts cards from its hand or graveyard when applicable under their instructions.
Proceed to combat. Horde creatures have haste and must attack if able.
The Horde has unlimited mana. Make any required choices as randomly as possible among legal options. Its spells and abilities still interact with the normal Magic stack.
The archived snapshot does not separately state a universal blocking restriction; do not silently import HordeMagic.com's defender-only restriction into it.
Damage, life loss, and life gain
The Horde has no life total. Damage or life loss that would affect it mills that many cards from its library.
Lifelink works for survivor creatures: damage can both mill the Horde and gain survivor life. Horde life gain does not return milled cards to its library in this recorded version.
Winning and losing
Survivors win when all three conditions hold:
The Horde library is empty.
The Horde hand is empty.
The Horde controls no creatures.
This differs from the HordeMagic.com requirement to clear its entire battlefield. A noncreature Horde permanent does not, by itself, prevent this snapshot's victory condition.
The Horde wins when shared survivor life reaches zero or less.
Recorded survivor ban list
Aether Flash; Aurification; Barbed Foliage; Caltrops; Crawlspace; Dueling Grounds; Dread; Elesh Norn, Grand Cenobite; Ensnaring Bridge; Eradicate; Grindstone; Haunting Echoes; Island Sanctuary; Lethal Vapors; Leyline of Singularity; Magus of the Moat; Mind Funeral; Moat; No Mercy; Platinum Angel; Platinum Emperion; Silent Arbiter; Solitary Confinement; Stormtide Leviathan; Surgical Extraction; Tainted Aether; Teferi's Moat; Time Stretch; Trepanation Blade; Urabrask the Hidden.
Apply the underlying survivor deck format's restrictions too.
Optional difficulty changes
The snapshot proposes the following adjustable rules. Choose and state their values before play:
Change the number of survivor setup turns.
Change each survivor's starting-life contribution.
Randomly remove a specified portion of the Horde before play.
Change the Horde's card list or use a defined sideboard.
Replace random Horde decisions with a survivor-consensus decision procedure.
Let Horde token cards remain in the graveyard instead of ceasing to exist.
Permit or prohibit attacks during survivor setup turns.
Changing token-to-spell ratios is also a deck-design adjustment. A boxed set must state the actual chosen settings rather than merely saying its difficulty is adjusted.
Source: the repository's archived wiki notes, attributed there to MTG Wiki's Horde Magic rules.

title: Building and Labeling Custom Jumpstart Packets
text:
Building and Labeling Custom Jumpstart Packets
Jumpstart parent page · Full play rules · Preparation guide: this catalogue's reusable custom boxes
Build the packets before game night so both setup and cleanup are quick. Each packet is a reusable twenty-card half-deck. Players combine two, play using the two-packet rules, then sort them back into their original packets.
The building preferences and sleeve method here are local conventions for our custom boxes. They do not change the underlying Magic rules or require retail Jumpstart packets to use the same card-selection constraints.
Choose a theme and a game plan
Give each packet a recognizable theme and a short description of how it plays. A character group, creature type, mechanical theme, or setting can provide the identity; the selected cards still need to work together on the table.
Choose the box's power level, intended players, and card pool before assembling packets. Cards can come from different sets and compatible settings. Ordinary card rules still apply: a robot-looking Construct remains a Construct, for example, and only receives a Robot-specific benefit if its actual types or a card effect qualify it.
The base format remains the starting point. Add a box-specific rule only when it serves a clear purpose, and write its procedure and scope on the box's page. A theme by itself does not create a rules exception.
Build exactly twenty cards, including lands
Choose the packet's colors. A single-color packet is an accessible starting point because another packet can supply a second color.
Start with a proposed balance of twelve nonland cards and eight lands, then adjust the contents after playing. This is a design starting point, not a universal Jumpstart requirement; the packet must still total twenty cards.
Include enough early plays, ways to interact, and ways to finish a game. Spread the mana costs so the packet can contribute before its most expensive card becomes castable.
Supply lands that cast this packet's spells while leaving room for the other packet to function. Check demanding colored costs and include suitable fixing where needed.
Keep synergy useful with a variety of partners. A packet should have a functioning plan without requiring one exact partner or one card to appear in every opening hand.
Record every card and quantity, including lands. Store tokens, counters, theme cards, and explanatory aids separately from the twenty deck cards.
Multicolor packets need enough mana support to work with their intended partners. If a packet only works with specific partners, list those combinations on its divider and on the box page before players choose. Do not promise unrestricted mixing for a box that has not been built for it.
The designer supplies complete packets; players do not add lands or repair their decks between selecting packets and starting a game.
Prefer variety; explain duplicates
Our default is one copy of each nonbasic card across packets that can be combined. Basic lands can repeat. Use different cards that perform related jobs to support a theme while keeping the individual cards varied.
A duplicate can be justified by a specific mechanical need, such as an essential engine piece or a strategy that depends on repeated copies of a particular card. Record the reason in the packet's design notes. A card being the most efficient option, or having many spare copies available, is not by itself the reason to include it repeatedly.
This is a custom-box design preference. Official packets can contain duplicates, and combining those packets does not require removing them. An exception in a custom box should be deliberate and recorded rather than silently changing the preference.
Give every physical packet a distinct identity
Prepare one identifier per packet, not just one identifier for the whole box. Two Spider-themed packets need different identifiers so they can be separated after being shuffled together.
A small thematic image can identify a packet. For example, a Spider-Verse packet could use a distinctive Spider-themed face or emblem. Add a short code or number when several packets use related artwork: MV-03 is a sample packet code, not a Magic set code. Keep identifiers unique across any boxes intended to be mixed.
Put the same identifier on:
Every one of the packet's twenty cards, using the sleeve method below.
Its divider, storage pocket, or container.
Its complete packet list.
The divider should also show the packet's name, colors, game plan, and any pairing restrictions. Keep the card list available for replacing a missing card or updating the packet, rather than requiring players to compare every card against it during routine cleanup.
Materials
The complete twenty-card packet, including lands.
Twenty clear inner sleeves that fit inside the chosen outer sleeves.
Twenty opaque-backed outer sleeves, identical to those on every packet that can be combined.
Twenty small stickers bearing the packet's identifier, plus a matching marker for its divider or container.
The packet list, storage divider or container, and required tokens or counters.
The stickers can be thematic rather than transparent. Choose small, flat labels that fit in a front corner without hiding information needed to play. Avoid raised or bulky decorations that distort the sleeve. The outer sleeve will protect the sticker's edge during shuffling, so the sticker does not have to withstand direct contact with other cards on its own.
Double-sleeve and mark every card
Put each card into a clear inner sleeve.
Apply its packet sticker to the outside front surface of that inner sleeve, near the bottom-left corner. The adhesive goes on the sleeve, never on the card.
Keep the marker clear of the card's name, mana cost, rules text, and power/toughness or loyalty information. Adjust its size and placement if the card's layout needs it.
Put the sleeved card into an opaque-backed outer sleeve. The marker is visible through the clear front and protected between the two sleeves, where it cannot catch directly on another card while shuffling.
Repeat for all twenty cards, including basic lands. Use a consistent marker size and position throughout the box, and keep the backs and edges indistinguishable across packets.
Mark the packet divider or container with the same identifier and confirm the completed packet contains twenty cards.
Identical outer sleeves preserve hidden information when two packets are shuffled together. Different sleeve backs would reveal packet membership in a library or an opponent's hand, so they are not this guide's default cleanup method. A box adopting that different information rule must say so explicitly.
These are permanent packet-identification labels, not Magic's in-game sticker mechanic. They do not add abilities or change a card's characteristics.
Try the method on two packets first. Check that the combined deck shuffles comfortably, the labels remain readable, card information is visible, and the sleeves sit flat before preparing the rest of the box.
Playtest the combinations and the cleanup
Test each packet with several intended partners, including same-color and different-color combinations where those are supported. Check whether players can cast their spells, participate early, interact with each other, and finish games. Also check whether one packet or combination consistently overwhelms the rest.
Keep adjustments within ordinary card and format rules whenever possible. Change the card selection, mana support, or pairing restrictions when those solve the issue. Record a new box-specific rule only if it is actually needed, with enough detail that another group can apply it without guessing.
Test putting the packets away as part of the same session. The intended reset is:
Recover all deck cards from every zone and return any borrowed or controlled cards to their physical packets. Restore double-faced cards to their front faces.
Set aside tokens and other play aids.
Sort the cards into piles by their visible packet markers.
Count twenty cards in each pile, including lands.
Put each pile behind its matching divider or into its matching container.
Use the saved list to resolve missing cards, an incorrect count, or a damaged marker. Repair those issues before the packet goes back into the selection pool. When replacing a card or sleeve, restore its packet marker and update the list if the contents changed.
What the boxed-set page records
A finished Jumpstart box should list:
The two-packet play rules as its base, or a different complete ruleset if it changes that procedure.
Its supported player count, packet inventory, and each packet's identifier and twenty-card list. Supply at least two physical packets per simultaneous player.
How players select packets and which combinations are supported.
Any deliberate duplicate cards and their design reasons.
Every additional or replacement game rule, including its timing and exact effect.
Required tokens, counters, dividers, and the marking and reset instructions.
The goal is a complete box that can be taken off the shelf, played, and put away again. Buying new cards or following later set releases is not part of its play procedure.
References
Wizards' Jumpstart overview and FAQ establishes the two twenty-card packets, with lands included.
Official Jumpstart decklists provide examples of packet construction.
How to Build Your Own Jumpstart Magic Environment discusses custom packet construction and the common eight-land starting point.
The preference for variety, protected thematic sleeve markers, and reusable-box reset process are local preparation conventions agreed for this catalogue.

title: Two-Packet Jumpstart
text:
Two-Packet Jumpstart
Jumpstart parent page · Rules: two prepared packets per player, using ordinary two-player Magic
Players and materials
This ruleset is for two players. Each player needs two Jumpstart packets, for four packets total. Each packet contains twenty playable cards, including its lands. Theme cards, packet dividers, tokens, and ordinary reminder inserts are kept separately and do not count toward those twenty cards.
Supply life counters and any tokens, counters, or other components required by the cards. Use official packets or a prepared custom box with complete twenty-card packet lists. A custom packet is built before the play session using the packet-building guide.
Jumpstart's deck-assembly procedure comes from the official product. The opening-hand and game procedures below use ordinary two-player Magic. If an event or box specifies a different procedure, such as a free first mulligan, that is an explicit addition to this version.
Select packets
Identify the available packet pool and read any box-specific pairing restrictions before distributing packets.
Give each player two complete packets. With unopened retail boosters, each player opens their two boosters. With a reusable box, use the box's stated selection method. If it has none, shuffle its packet-divider cards face down and deal two to each player, then take the matching packets.
Set aside the theme cards, dividers, tokens, and other non-deck inserts.
Each player may inspect their own two packets before combining them. A known packet list does not reveal the order of the shuffled deck.
The face-down divider deal is this catalogue's default for distributing a reusable collection; buying random boosters is not required. A box may instead allow players to choose themes or draft whole packets, but it must supply that selection procedure. The unselected packets remain outside the game.
Assemble the decks
Combine all twenty cards from each selected packet into a single forty-card deck.
Keep the lands that came with both packets. There is no separate land-adding or card-cutting step.
Keep each player's deck, library, hand, graveyard, and other zones separate from their opponent's.
The combined deck is not a pool from which to choose a smaller deck. Do not replace cards from unused packets or a personal collection during the game. This setup supplies no sideboard or extra companion card.
Two packets of the same color or theme can be combined. Copies of a card supplied by the two packets remain in the deck; Jumpstart does not impose singleton or the constructed four-copy restriction on the contents of those packets. This catalogue's preference to design custom packets with few duplicates is a preparation choice, not a rule that removes cards from official packets.
Cards from different Jumpstart releases can be combined. Custom boxes can define their own card pools, but should state any restrictions before players select packets. A card's legality in Standard or Commander is not an additional restriction on this Jumpstart game.
Set up the game
Randomly determine who chooses which player takes the first turn, using a die roll, coin flip, or another agreed method.
Each player starts at 20 life.
Each player thoroughly shuffles their combined deck and offers it to their opponent to cut or shuffle. It becomes their library.
Each player draws seven cards.
Resolve mulligans as described below.
Resolve any actions a card permits from an opening hand, in starting-player order, then begin the first turn.
Mulligans
Use the normal London mulligan for a two-player game:
Starting with the player taking the first turn, each player declares whether to keep their hand or take a mulligan.
Each player taking a mulligan shuffles their hand back into their library and draws seven cards again.
That player puts a number of cards equal to their total number of mulligans on the bottom of their library in any order: one after their first mulligan, two after their second, and so on.
Repeat for players who still want to mulligan. A player who keeps their hand takes no further mulligans. Stop when everyone has kept, or a player's opening hand would be zero cards.
This version has no free first mulligan. A mulligan changes the opening hand, not the selected packets or deck contents.
Turns, spells, and combat
The starting player skips the draw step of their first turn. After that exception, players alternate ordinary Magic turns, with the normal beginning phase, first main phase, combat phase, second main phase, and ending phase.
Use normal land-play limits, mana costs, spell timing, priority, combat, and card text. Jumpstart supplies no extra mana, shared resources, free spells, or special combat procedure. The shared rules reference explains the underlying Magic rules assumed by the catalogue.
Legendary creatures are shuffled into the deck like other cards. They do not become commanders. There is no commander selection, command-zone casting, commander tax, commander damage, or Commander color-identity restriction. Ordinary rules such as the legend rule still apply.
Packet labels and sleeve stickers are sorting aids. They do not change a card's name, color, types, abilities, or ownership, and they do not authorize looking at a hidden card. A thematic character or team label does not grant an ability that is absent from the actual card.
Winning and losing
Normal Magic victory and loss conditions apply. A player normally loses when they have zero or less life, have ten or more poison counters, attempt to draw more cards than remain in their library, or are made to lose by a card effect. They may also concede. Merely having an empty library does not cause a loss until a required draw cannot be completed.
When one player loses, the other wins. Card effects can provide other ways to win or modify a loss condition. If both players lose simultaneously, the game is a draw. Jumpstart adds no separate scoring, boss objective, or alternate victory condition.
Another game
The procedure above plays a single game. Players may shuffle the same pair of packets for a rematch or reset the packets and select new combinations.
If playing a match with the same decks, agree on its length before starting. The loser of the previous game chooses who takes the first turn in the next game. After a drawn game, the player who made that choice previously makes it again. Keep the selected forty-card decks intact between games unless the box explicitly defines a different match structure.
Reset a reusable box
Collect cards from every zone, including cards that changed controllers, were exiled, or were set aside to represent another card. Restore double-faced cards to their front faces for sorting.
Remove tokens, counters, and other non-deck components.
Sort the cards face up by their packet markers, including the basic lands. Each physical packet has its own identifier.
Count twenty cards per packet, then return each packet to its matching divider or container.
If a count is wrong or a marker is missing, check that packet's stored list before returning it to the available pool.
The preparation guide explains how to protect the markers inside sleeves. Its decklists are a reference for missing cards and changes; ordinary cleanup uses the markers and a card count.
Sources
Wizards' Jumpstart overview and FAQ: two themed twenty-card packets, lands included, combined into one forty-card deck.
Introducing Jumpstart: the original packet-based play structure.
Official Jumpstart decklists: examples of complete packet contents and multiple versions of a theme.
Magic Comprehensive Rules, especially 100.2b, 103, and 104: Limited deck construction, starting the game, mulligans, and game-ending conditions.
The reusable-box distribution fallback and packet-reset procedure are catalogue conventions. The custom-packet guide records the owner's preparation preferences; they are not requirements imposed on every official Jumpstart product.

title: Feudalism
text:
Feudalism
All boxed sets · BANG-like format family
The recurring-monarchy concept below is recorded. The specific base ruleset, role distribution, and victory conditions have not been chosen. This page does not silently adopt one source's roles or invent a finished ruleset.
Concept
Feudalism is a hidden-role game-night box built around the monarch mechanic. Players can fight over the crown, but power returns to the King until the group breaks that structure. A Renegade-style role is intended to win by properly dethroning the King; what qualifies as dethroning still needs a rule.
Base ruleset
Not yet selected. Choose a specific version before this box can be played:
BANG! Magic: Sheriff, Deputies, Outlaws, and Renegade.
Kingdoms: King, Knight, Bandits, Assassin, and optional Usurper.
Kingdom / BANG EDH: Emperor, Guard, Assassins, and Rogue.
MTG Treachery: custom identities with unveil abilities.
These versions have different victory and reveal rules. Choosing one is a design decision, not merely renaming its leader to King.
Recorded additional rules
F1. Starting monarchy
The player with the King role starts the game as the monarch.
F2. The crown returns
At the start of the King's turn, if the King is not the monarch, the King becomes the monarch.
The original concept says “at the start of the King's turn.” Before playtesting, decide whether this happens before untapping or as a triggered ability at the beginning of upkeep. Those timings behave differently; no timing has been chosen here.
F3. Ordinary monarchy
The King role and being the monarch are different things. The recorded rule changes who has the monarch designation; it does not say that taking the monarch designation changes a hidden role.
Unless the completed box explicitly replaces them, the ordinary monarch rules apply:
Exactly one player is the monarch once the designation has entered the game. A new monarch replaces the previous one.
At the beginning of the monarch's end step, the monarch's inherent ability triggers and that player draws a card when it resolves.
When a creature deals combat damage to the monarch, an inherent ability triggers; when it resolves, that creature's controller becomes the monarch.
If the monarch leaves the game, the active player becomes the monarch. If the active player is leaving too, the next player in turn order becomes the monarch.
These are ordinary monarch rules, checked against the official rulings for Palace Jailer. They do not define Feudalism's dethroning victory condition.
Replacement rules still to design
Rule area
Required decision
Player count and roles
Name every role and give an exact distribution for each supported player count.
Victory
State every role's win/loss condition, what dethroning means, and which result takes precedence if conditions coincide.
King bonuses
Decide starting life, opening hand size, and any bonus beyond recurring monarchy.
Crown timing
Choose the exact timing and whether players can respond to F2.
Revealing roles
Decide whether becoming monarch reveals a role or triggers any role-specific ability.
Leaving the game
Decide how eliminating or replacing the King affects F2, the remaining roles, and the end of the game.
Deck and component requirements
The recorded deck requirements are:
Every deck features monarch cards or cards that care about becoming the monarch.
Every deck works with any role it might receive.
The decks encourage contesting the crown while leaving the King vulnerable to pressure.
Deck count, decklists, supported player counts, role cards, and starting-life aids remain to be specified. Include a monarch marker and a reminder for F2 when preparing the first playtest kit.
Optional rules
No optional module has been finalized. Proposed role triggers, alternate King bonuses, or different crown rules belong here once their complete procedures are written down.
References
The original concept is preserved in this repository's history. Its source family is documented under BANG-like hidden roles and source notes.

title: New York Animal Invasion
text:
New York Animal Invasion
All boxed sets · Horde format family
New York is invaded by ordinary animals, and ordinary people face the invasion. This is the planned first Horde box; the first box being designed overall is Zombies vs Plants: Jumpstart. Horde design and playtesting are deferred. No base ruleset, decks, or complete play procedure has been selected for this concept.
Premise
Make mundane animals and ordinary New Yorkers the focus of a cooperative Horde game. The animal side supplies the invasion; the people's side represents residents dealing with it. Everyday places and activities establish the New York setting.
This is a theme direction, not a change to any card's name, type, abilities, or rules text. The existing research offers candidates, not an approved card pool or a decklist.

Zombies vs Plants: Jumpstart
All boxed sets · Jumpstart · Browse card research
Eight complete packets are ready for initial testing. Their balance, mana, and partner compatibility are not yet established. The selection procedure below is this box's local draft rule, not an official Jumpstart product rule.
The box
Two players face off as Plants versus Zombies. Each player combines two different twenty-card packets from their faction into a forty-card deck. Each v0.1 packet contains twelve nonland cards and eight lands; a combined deck therefore has twenty-four nonlands and sixteen lands.
The Plant packets are Overgrowth (green Plants), Ancient Grove (white Treefolk and canopy allies), Spore Swarm (black living Fungi), and Wild Awakening (green animated lands). The Zombie packets are Restless Dead (black necromancy), Stitched Together (blue laboratory creations), Tomb Guard (white mummies), and The Turned (green Zombies, especially undead vegetation).
Drafted October 21, 2026. Jump to the eight lists · Packet lists and design notes (JSON) · Card text snapshot (JSON) · Whole-box inventory (TXT)
Each packet section has a plain-text list. To load a forty-card deck into a deck-list importer, combine the text of two legal packets. The whole-box inventory is for assembling all eight packets, not a playable deck. No physical price target has been set; these are gameplay drafts, not a purchasing recommendation.
First playtest recorded: Overgrowth + Spore Swarm played Restless Dead + The Turned. See the interaction findings and proposed swaps, or browse the interaction candidates. The lists below remain the v0.1 baseline; the proposed changes are not yet applied.
Base rules and box changes
Use Two-Packet Jumpstart for the underlying game. This box adds ZP1, the same-faction restriction, and replaces the base rules' unrestricted packet deal with ZP2, the faction assignment and selection procedure below. Everything else uses ordinary Magic and the base rules, including spell timing, responses, combat, and victory conditions.
ZP1. Both packets must belong to the same faction
Each packet has a fixed Plant or Zombie label. A player's two packets must have matching faction labels, but do not need matching colors, creature types, or strategies. Supporting spells belong to their packet's faction. Labels do not grant card types or abilities.
Undead botanical creatures belong to Zombies. Plant Zombies, Zombie Treefolk, Zombie Fungi, and botanical undead flavor picks belong on that side. Living Fungi and Saprolings belong to Plants; using sacrifice or graveyard mechanics does not itself make a card undead. Cards keep their actual Oracle types and colors.
ZP2. Assign factions and select packets
Set out the four Plant packet dividers and four Zombie packet dividers, with each complete packet stored behind its matching divider.
Assign one player to Plants and one to Zombies by agreement. If there is no agreement, flip a coin: the winner chooses a faction and the other player receives the remaining faction. In the playtest application, set these assignments before opening packet selection.
Each player inspects the four packet lists in their assigned faction and chooses two different packets. Confirm those choices, take the matching packets, and set the other packets aside. In the application, players confirm in seat order; the coordinator opens ordinary game setup after both have confirmed.
Combine all forty cards, including all sixteen supplied lands. Do not cut cards, add lands, borrow cards from unused packets, or add outside upgrades. Dividers, tokens, and counters are not deck cards.
Randomly determine which player chooses who takes the first turn, independently of the faction-assignment coin flip. Set each player's life total to 20. Shuffle each deck and offer the opponent a cut.
Draw seven cards each, then take mulligans as below. The starting player skips their first draw step.
Controlled playtests: the host may specify particular pairs before selection, so a weak pairing can receive repeated tests. For random variety instead, shuffle each faction’s four dividers face down and draw two without replacement. Record whether pairs were player-chosen, host-assigned, or randomly dealt. These options change only selection; each faction still supplies two different intact packets. The current application implements player choice, with host assignments communicated in the setup instructions or chat.
This draft is a two-player Plants-versus-Zombies game. Same-faction mirror matches, multiplayer, duplicate-packet decks, and three-packet decks are outside its current procedure. Mulligans never change packet selection.
Mulligans, turns, and winning
Use the normal London mulligan, with no free first mulligan. In starting-player order, each player decides whether to keep or mulligan. A player who mulligans shuffles their hand into their library and draws seven again; when they keep, they put one card on the bottom of their library for each mulligan they took. Repeat for players still taking mulligans; a player who has kept does not rejoin. Stop at a kept hand of zero cards at the latest.
Play ordinary Magic: untap, upkeep, draw, first main phase, combat, second main phase, and ending phase. Use the normal one-land-per-turn limit unless a card changes it, normal costs, timing, priority, and combat. Each deck is the combined pair, not two separately played halves. Legendary creatures are ordinary deck cards, not commanders. Normal losses include having 0 or less life, ten poison counters, being unable to complete a required draw, a card effect, or conceding. When one player loses, the other wins; simultaneous losses produce a draw. An empty library alone is not a loss. Card effects and the base rules govern exceptions; the factions add no alternate victory condition.
The default session is one game. For another game, either keep the same pairs and repeat setup, or reset the packets and repeat selection. A best-of match is only used if agreed beforehand; use the base rules' match procedure for choosing the starting player in subsequent games.

Creeperhulk sets base power and toughness to 5/5 and grants trample for the turn. Counters and other bonuses still apply; defender stays, so Jaddi Offshoot and Gatecreeper Vine still cannot attack.

Fists of Ironwood needs a legal creature target to resolve and enter before producing its two Saprolings. The enchanted creature can be either player’s creature.
Abundant Growth fixes color but does not add mana or change land types. Ilysian Caryatid must be able to use its tap ability; it produces two mana of one color if you control a creature with power at least four.

First-test watch points
Creeperhulk can make birds or Saprolings into very efficient finishers. Measure whether this one card decides too many games.
Two defenders and a mana creature make some opening hands passive. Bayou Groff is not a normal two-drop without fodder.

Hoofprints of the Stag is an enchantment, not an early creature. Each card drawn can give it one hoofprint counter. Pay 2W and remove four counters to make a 4/4 white flying Elemental, only during your turn.

Indomitable Ancients and Old Ghastbark provide toughness more than offensive power. Check whether board stalls outweigh the flying and buff finishers.
Hoofprints requires several draws and another mana payment before providing a body. The birds and partner’s early creatures must cover that delay.

The three reusable sacrifice outlets are intentionally paid outlets (Mold Folk, Soothsayer, Omnivore), so they compete for mana rather than enabling an unrestricted free-sacrifice engine. Choose one outlet for the resource you actually need.
Mold Folk's lifelink and Thallid Omnivore's Saproling sacrifice can enable Brackish Trudge's return ability. Without life gain it remains a three-mana 4/2 that enters tapped.
Fungal Fortitude can save a nontoken creature through a death and retrigger an entry/death ability. The Aura does not return attached; tokens do not return after dying.

Playing the packet
Five creature cards, seven noncreature spells, eight lands. Five cards animate lands when counting Awakener Druid and Embodiment of Insight, so creature-card count understates its eventual board presence.
Leafkin Druid, Dawntreader Elk, and Fertilid provide early presence without an Elf package. Dawntreader Elk is a deliberate woodland-animal support choice rather than a literal botanical creature.
Land animation usually does not untap the land. Pay for spells or abilities with other sources when you want the animated land to attack or block.
A land that became a creature this turn may attack or use a tap ability if you have controlled it continuously since your turn began; becoming a creature does not by itself reset that history. Newly played lands need haste while they are creatures.
Awakener Druid and Genju do not grant haste. Nissa's Zendikon, Rampaging Growth, and Embodiment of Insight do. Awakener's Forest stops being a creature when the Druid leaves; Genju and Embodiment animations end at end of turn.
Nissa's Zendikon returns the enchanted land card to hand when that land dies; the Aura goes to the graveyard. Genju can recover its Aura when the enchanted Forest goes to a graveyard, not the Forest itself.
Rampaging Growth puts a basic land onto the battlefield untapped unless something else changes that. It has reach and haste as a 4/3 Insect until end of turn, and remains a land afterward.
Ash Barrens supplies colorless if played; for fixing, pay one generic mana to discard it with basic landcycling and find a basic land in hand. That is not an extra land play.
Cultivate, Elk, and Fertilid can find a partner's basic Plains or Swamp, whereas Genju and Awakener specifically require an actual Forest.
First-test watch points
Land creatures expose the mana base to ordinary creature removal. Five actual creature cards should be checked against each partner for hands containing support but no useful attacker.
Several animation durations and sizes require clear markers; the rules notes should be near the list. Avoid stacking multiple animation effects on one land unless necessary.
Ram Through needs a creature with useful power. Do not spend all available mana animating a land and leave no mana to cast it.
Ramp density may flood a combined deck or run out of basic lands to find; adjust one ramp spell or a land after playtesting rather than assuming eight lands is final.
Retained alternatives: Animate Land — Replaced by Fertilid to improve actual creature count and early development. Living Lands / Natural Affinity / Kormus Bell — Affect opposing lands and create excessive risk and board bookkeeping. Life and Limb — Global type interactions and possible compulsory token loops are too complex for this first draft. Awakening of Vitu-Ghazi — A nine-counter 9/9 is a much larger power spike than the chosen threats. Woodcaller Automaton — Prototype adds another casting/size system; retain as a future alternative. Sylvan Advocate / Llanowar Loamspeaker — Useful efficient options, but non-Elf alternatives preserve the owner's theme preference. Playing the packet
All main spell costs and repeat-use costs require only one blue pip.
Headless Skaab cannot be cast unless a creature card can be exiled from your graveyard as its additional cost, and it enters tapped. Screeching Skaab, Selhoff Entomber, Organ Hoarder, and normal creature trades supply material.
Selhoff Entomber can discard only a creature card. It cannot discard a spare land or spell for its tap ability.
Exploit on Stitched Assistant is optional. If using it, the sacrificed creature may be the Assistant itself; sacrifice only when the card and scry are worth the lost body.
Stitchwing Skaab returns tapped from the graveyard for 1U plus discarding two cards; this is an activated ability, not casting it again.
Think Twice's flashback is another spell casting and exiles the spell afterward; it can be used after ordinary casting or after being milled.
Compelling Deterrence can target your own permanent, but if you control a Zombie its owner then discards too. Normally use it on the opponent.
Essence Scatter answers a creature spell on the stack, not a creature already on the battlefield.
Sleep Paralysis keeps its target from untapping during its controller's untap step while the Aura remains attached; it is not destruction.
No tokens or +1/+1 counters required by the blue packet itself. No nonbasic duplicates.
First-test watch points
There is no one-drop, so all three two-drop bodies matter for early play. Check blue+green and blue+white starts rather than relying solely on black's one-drops.
Headless Skaab can be stranded in hand without a creature in the graveyard. If this happens too often, replace it with a standalone creature instead of adding more mill solely to force it.
One exile cost and a recurring flyer are deliberately the limit; don't add Skaab Ruinator or multiple corpse-consuming creatures before checking graveyard availability.
Blue+black is likely to have the most recursion/card advantage. Blue+white must still work through its normal bodies, tempo, and its own graveyard payoffs.
Discarding two cards to return Stitchwing Skaab is expensive and shouldn't be treated as free card advantage.
Retained alternatives: Armored Skaab — A second heavier mandatory self-mill source is unnecessary; Seagraf Skaab supplies a simpler defensive body. Geralf, Visionary Stitcher — Global Zombie flying and scalable sacrifice tokens are too strong/complex for the first fair comparison. Hordewing Skaab — Global Zombie flying can erase the intended contrast with the Plant faction's grounded big creatures. Cleaver Skaab — Copy-token engines and repeated entry triggers are a later balancing experiment. Falcon Abomination — Useful flyer, but decayed introduces another token rule; Stitchwing supplies evasive pressure without that subsystem. Rooftop Nuisance — Casualty creates spell copies and sacrifice sequencing; Sleep Paralysis is simpler sustained interaction. Forbidden Alchemy — Its flashback requires a black partner; Think Twice works fully with every pairing. Skaab Ruinator — Exiling three creature cards and repeated graveyard casting demands too much dedicated support.

Playing the packet
Sacred Cat begins as a living Cat, not a Zombie. It is the packet's one deliberately chosen living creature: its embalm turns it into an ancient-tomb mummy, giving a simple introduction to the theme's return-from-death mechanic.
Embalm costs W, is activated only at sorcery speed from the graveyard, and exiles the original Sacred Cat card. Create a white 1/1 Zombie Cat token with lifelink and no mana cost; it is not the original card returned. Its entry triggers Binding Mummy and Mummy Paramount.
Fan Bearer must be able to tap and costs2 mana to activate. To prevent a creature attacking, tap it before attackers are declared; tapping an already-attacking creature does not remove it from combat.
Time to Reflect requires its target to have blocked or been blocked by a Zombie during the current turn. Casting it after blockers are declared but before damage can save a creature; it cannot exile an unrelated creature.
Mummy Paramount's bonus is temporary, not a +1/+1 counter. Binding Mummy triggers for another Zombie, not itself.
Unconventional Tactics is a sorcery. A Zombie entering can return it from the graveyard only after its controller pays W; its +3/+3 and flying last for the turn.
Cast Out's exile ends when the enchantment leaves. It can be cast with flash, and its cycling option costs W and discarding the card.

First-test watch points
Only modest base power on its creatures; wins may depend too heavily on a partner's large threat or In Oketra's Name. Adjust after tests rather than prematurely adding a powerful lord.
Cast Out and Time to Reflect are the main creature answers; flyers can otherwise evade the ground mummies.
Sacred Cat's lifelink and double body add resilience, while the rare absence of a Zombie in early hands can delay tribal payoffs.

Playing the packet
Every spell is castable using green mana. Slitherhead and Sludge Titan are black-green cards with hybrid mana costs, but their symbols can all be paid with green. Their actual colors remain black and green.
The two repeated nonbasic cards are intentional: two Slitherheads and two Sultai Devotees preserve an actual-Zombie early curve without adding radiation, foretell, or obligate off-color cards. All other nonbasic cards are singleton within the Zombie faction.
Slitherhead's scavenge costs 0, exiles that card from the graveyard, and is activated only at sorcery speed. The resulting counter can help any creature. Removing the card means it no longer discounts a Ghoultree that has not been cast.
Sultai Devotee is a 2/1 with deathtouch. Its once-per-turn ability pays 1 to produce B, G, or U: this is filtering, not extra mana or a tap ability. Its body functions without using that ability.
Ghoultree costs one generic mana less for each creature card in its controller's graveyard, down to a minimum of G. It has no trample by itself; Rancor supplies that role.
Sludge Titan's mill 5 is mandatory whenever it enters or attacks. Recovery of a creature and/or land among those five cards is optional. Choosing not to attack can avoid another mill trigger. It does not recover arbitrary older graveyard cards.
Mulch reveals four and puts lands into hand, other cards into the graveyard; it does not put lands directly onto the battlefield. Grapple's recovery can choose any creature or land card already in the graveyard, not just its newly milled cards.
Ram Through deals damage from the chosen friendly creature, not from the spell itself. Deathtouch is therefore relevant; damage to the opposing player only arises from its trample clause.
Rancor returns only when it goes from the battlefield to a graveyard; an Aura spell that never entered does not trigger that return.
Thriving Grove is not a Forest. It enters tapped and chooses a nongreen color as it enters; ordinarily choose the partner's mana color.
First-test watch points
This half has six creatures and no natural three- or four-mana creature. Every other Zombie half must contribute enough middle-curve bodies; assess the combined deck, not this half alone.
Sludge Titan repeatedly mills five cards in a forty-card deck. This is the main deliberate test risk, especially paired with blue. Track remaining library and do not attack automatically. If games are frequently lost to self-mill, replace Titan first rather than quietly changing its rules.
Scavenge, Regrowth, Grapple, and a partner's recursion/exile costs all remove resources that may be needed for Ghoultree's discount.
Rancor plus deathtouch/trample or Ram Through can be potent. Test its power against the largely ground-based Plant faction and do not assume low mana cost implies low impact.
Rancor and Ram Through need a creature; creature-light opening hands can leave support inactive. This is another reason for the two approved duplicate exceptions.
Retained alternatives: Dreg Mangler; Shambling Shell; Skullbriar; Molderhulk; The Necrobloom — Retained in research, but these need off-color mana and cannot assume a specific partner. God-Eternal Rhonas — Power-doubling, vigilance, deathtouch, and unusual library return make a high-impact and busy baseline finisher. The Foretold Soldier — Forced-blocking, damage/exile, foretell, and recasting loop add unnecessary complexity. Glowing One; Tato Farmer — Radiation adds an unrelated subsystem. Moldervine Cloak — Dredge adds another draw-replacement/mill decision; Rancor fills the boost/evasion role with a simpler recurring Aura. A second Ghoultree — Adds another slow opening-hand card rather than improving the early curve.
Physical inventory and reset
The box contains 160 deck cards: 96 nonlands and 64 lands, stored as eight separately identified twenty-card packets, plus eight matching dividers. Supply the tokens and counters listed with the packets, two life trackers, and a coin or die. Tokens and other play aids remain outside the 160-card inventory.
Use the packet preparation guide to mark every card, including basic lands, with its packet identifier. Use matching opaque outer sleeves throughout the box so that packet membership cannot be distinguished from card backs. Keep a versioned inventory with each packet.
After a game, collect cards from every zone, including any borrowed by the other player. Remove tokens and counters, then sort cards by packet identifier. Restore every packet to its exact listed twenty cards, including its lands, and return its divider. Check counts and resolve missing or misplaced cards before returning the packets to the pool. Restore any double-faced cards to their front faces before storage.
Tokens and markers
Supply several copies or clearly labeled substitutes for repeatable tokens; the number of supplied token cards never limits how many the game can create.

Design boundaries
The first draft favors familiar combat, useful early creatures, and a small number of mechanics. Each packet is half a deck and should contribute a useful plan with each of its three same-faction partners. Ancient Grove's Treefolk supply larger threats; its literal birds and supporting Druid help it participate early. Humanoid Bird people are not part of that canopy-support theme. Botanical Elementals, Dryads, and suitable noncreatures can support the Plant identities without changing their printed types.
Packets are built to function with one mana color. A hybrid card is acceptable when that color can pay its costs; this does not change the card's actual colors and does not invoke Commander color identity. Prefer singleton nonbasic cards across packets that can be combined. Any deliberate repeat should have a recorded thematic or functional reason; repeating expensive creatures does not repair an early curve.
All unused candidates remain in the shared research for rebalancing and the future cube. Multicolor packets, three-packet sixty-card decks, and optional spotlight cards remain separate ideas. This version has no upgrade pool, substitutions, special mana rule, or free casting. The Necrobloom and other appealing multicolor undead stay on the Zombie-side research wishlist until a separate construction and mana plan supports them. A future spotlight upgrade would need an eligible pair, exact card-and-land substitutions, a fair selection rule, and a reset inventory; none is enabled in v0.1. The ordinary-animal invasion of New York remains a separate future Horde box.
Pairing checks
These are design expectations to test, not results. Each packet has three legal partners; all six pairings in each faction are supported by the inventory.

Zombies

Ordinary Zombies trigger mummy payoffs; black supplies recursion and removal. Are tribal bonuses consistent without becoming overwhelming?

Mana: a Thriving land enters tapped and chooses its second color as it enters. Normally choose the other packet's color; in green-green, choose any permitted nongreen color and use the land for green. Thriving lands have no basic land type. Wild Awakening uses Ash Barrens plus basic-land searches instead; basic landcycling puts a land in hand, not onto the battlefield. No spell assumes another packet supplies a missing casting color.
Curve: the JSON includes printed mana-value counts, which do not capture Groff's extra cost, Ghoultree's discount, convoke, or the later payments needed for Hoofprints and land animation. Count usable early plays when reviewing hands, not just printed numbers.
Test and revise
Record box version, both packet pairs, starting player, result, and game log. Note mana problems, missed early plays, rules mistakes, stalled boards, memorable interactions, and cards that felt ineffective or overwhelming. Evaluate each packet with all three of its partners, including whether Ancient Grove gets enough early support and whether black Fungi functions without green.
Four packets yield six distinct pairs per faction, or 36 opposing pairings. Start with representative games, then repeat questionable pairings and swap which side starts. Distinguish a rules mistake or unusual draw from a repeated deck problem before changing cards. The aim is useful, approachable games rather than proving balance from a single result.
Keep v0.1 lists intact in the record. For each revision, record the changed card quantities and the reason, assign a new version, and update the packet inventories. Retain cut cards in research. Compare results against the exact versions played rather than combining different lists under one packet name.
